Continuous speech represents a complex and multidimensional perception, encompassing not only auditory cues but also visual and auditory cues from speech partners. Current state-of-the-art models for speech generation, including WaveNet and T5, have achieved notable success, yet they fail to incorporate a context-sensitive approach that accurately reflects the complexities of human communication. To address this limitation, we present ContextWaveNet, a context-sensitive model for speech generation, built on the foundation of WaveNet with an augmented convolutional layer that incorporates masking and contextual approaches. By contextualizing each audio token as a combination of its local and global contextualized representations, ContextWaveNet is able to capture refined, context-sensitive relationships. Our results from the FOLDAE benchmark demonstrate that ContextWaveNet outperforms WaveNet and T5 in terms of convergence speed and ultra-low frequency loss. Moreover, our analyses using SIPT and SIPT+ demonstrate the efficacy of ContextWaveNet in generating more natural and coherent speech, particularly in relation to its masked speech generation component. This study introduces a novel inference technique called hidden space mapping, which involves projecting an input model onto a secondary domain - the hidden space - using a non-invertible transformation. The hidden space is mapped to the standard probability space through an analysis-based mapping function. By applying this transformation, predictive inference can be performed in the hidden space and then converted back to the original variable space for usage. The method is initially developed for models with discrete and normal-distributed parameters, and subsequently extended to handle continuous and continuous-categorical variables. A set of conditions is proposed to ensure the reliability of the method, and it is demonstrated through the application of HS-MAP to various practical scenarios including predictive therapy modeling and clinical decision-making. Furthermore, the performance of HS-MAP is evaluated in multiple benchmark datasets where it is compared to other efficient inference techniques. Notably, the method exhibits superior efficiency and accuracy across various metrics such as prediction time, log-likelihood, and mean squared error. In particular, the Predictive Information Criterion (PIC) is found to be an effective tool for assessing the quality of maps and guiding the optimization of hyperparameters. The study includes a comprehensive implementation in DeepMap, an open-source Python package for efficient predictive inference. The package is designed to enhance the performance of machine learning models by facilitating the integration of domain expertise and easy replication, exemplified in the provided code. The package is freely available on GitHub. A reproducibility report and a tutorial on the application of HS-MAP are also provided. This includes a step-by-step guide to creating and evaluating the performance of models using DeepMap, and a set of code examples illustrating its usage in various scenarios. The study concludes by highlighting the potential future developments and applications of hidden space mapping, and suggesting several areas for further research and investigation. These include the extension of the method to model combinations, and the exploration of the theoretical underpinnings of the technique. Potential areas of application are also identified, and they encompass a broad range of domains including therapy, genetics, and content-based application domains. In particular, the method is found to be particularly useful in scenarios where compact representations of input models are desirable, and it exhibits great potential for further development and application in various contexts. Researchers introduced ADN, a generative model capable of creating fake neural network models that mimic existing ones, leading to a vulnerability in machine learning classifiers that can be exploited by manipulating the fake models to get approved fake data, thereby allowing attackers to control classification outcomes with high confidence. Our research revealed that ADN is not the only model capable of this attack, as other generative models, such as DNN and Normalization flows, can also create fake neural networks that pass as real. Furthermore, we found that fake neural network models can be effectively represented and learned from data without the need for sequential computation, as opposed to the initial assumption. We proposed FNC, a new generative model capable of creating fake neural networks that pass as real, confirmed its superiority over existing models in terms of performance and compatibility with various datasets. Our experiments and analysis on MNIST, EMNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrated that FNC is a more effective tool for launching person-in-the-middle attacks against machine learning classifiers in terms of performance and confidence levels. Our research also introduced three new approaches: Label-Learning, Inverse-Label, and Re-Labelling, designed to mitigate the vulnerability of deep learning classifiers from insider threats, as well as an adaptation of Re-Labelling using Federated Learning. Our findings show that these methods can significantly reduce the effectiveness of such attacks while maintaining the model's accuracy. Our research provides a framework for future research on insider threats, particularly on person-in-the-middle attacks, and opens up new areas of research within the deep learning and Federated Learning domains. Climate change denial patterns persist, especially online, where recent shifts in the US climate policy have sparked a surge in recent years. Contrary to typical denial patterns, the motivation behind these recent instances appears to stem from political ideology. Analyzing nearly 19 million social media posts from 2018 to 2020, our study examines the phenomenon and its underlying causes. Unlike conventional climate deniers, who often present a unified view, the new conspiracy myths are diverse and predominantly created by bots. They focus on the removal of climate questions from the study questions of the 9th grade science exam in New York City, demonstrating the success of targeted disinformation campaigns in spreading climate deception. Unlike traditional climate deniers, the new conspiracy myths are immune to standard counter-arguments and require an in-depth understanding of the specific context to effectively debunk them. To address this "new world" of climate disinformation, our study proposes a novel approach to analyzing disinformation that prioritizes user perspectives over general narratives. To aid in the practical application of our research, a full dataset is available for other researchers to utilize. Instrumental variables that aren't ranked can be analyzed using the "monotonic instrument" concept, which applies when an instrument's effect on the outcome variable is consistent and an individual's most instrumented variable is less than their actual variable. Although the monotonic instrument's existence condition appears complex, it has a simpler form when the instrument's effect on the outcome variable remains constant. Conditions for identifying the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome using the monotonic instrument involve two primary requirements. Firstly, the treated group must contain individuals who aren't treated with the instrument's minimum option. Secondly, the treated group must contain individuals who use the instrument's maximum option either by choice or through variation in preferences. If these conditions are met, the causal effect can be calculated by comparing the treated group's difference in outcomes between the highest and lowest treatment options with the untreated group's difference in outcomes between the lowest and highest treatment options. This concept was further demonstrated by analyzing the effects of disciplines of study on earnings using the monotonic instrument's conditions, with the instrument being the disciplines' order and the outcome being earnings. The analysis revealed that engineering and physical science graduates who studied through math have higher earnings than those who studied through language, with the opposite applying to graduates from personal and social studies. Furthermore, engineering and physical science graduates who studied through math have higher earnings than those who studied through language in both treated and untreated groups. These findings illustrate the practical utility of the monotonic instrument in identifying causal effects when instruments aren't ranked. The feasibility of producing antineutrons and various baryons at super J/psi factories will be explored, along with their applications in high-accuracy experiments. It is anticipated that a sufficient supply of these particles can be obtained using accelerator-based techniques. The implementation of a high-accuracy antineutron detector at the super J/psi factory will be designed, particularly with the intent of employing it as a target for high-precision antineutron decay searches, such as checking baryon number conservation. The antineutron detector's detection capabilities will also enable the detection of rare baryon decay modes, such as investigating the reliability of baryon strong interaction conservation. The antineutron detector will serve a broader purpose, supporting a variety of high-precision baryon physics research, including studies on baryon electromagnetic structure, baryon form factors, and rare baryon decays. Consequently, the establishment of a super J/psi factory coupled with an antineutron detector will provide unparalleled opportunities for high-precision baryon physics research, greatly surpassing the capabilities of existing facilities. This will be particularly evident in research concerning baryon electromagnetic structure and form factors, as well as in sensitive decay mode detections. The construction of an antineutron detector at a super J/psi factory will be a monumental undertaking, requiring significant technical and financial resources. However, it will yield a vast array of long-sought data in high-precision baryon physics research, thereby making the investment well-worth the expense. The proposed antineutron detector will be a cutting-edge, high-technology device, featuring advanced and sophisticated design elements, such as a large-scale, 60-meter-long, 3-meter-diameter antineutron beamline with multiple magnetic bends; a 1.2-meter-diameter, 30-meter-long target station with integrated, high-precision antineutron detectors; and a 1-meter-diameter, 5-meter-long decay channel with multi-layered, high-precision antineutron detector placement. The detector will also feature a 3-meter-diameter, 4-meter-high, segmented antineutron detector with more than 2000 units of the large-area, high-precision antineutron detectors. Furthermore, the antineutron detector will incorporate a series of the large-area, high-precision antineutron detectors at the end of the decay channel, totaling more than 300 units. To address the flatness problem in the early universe, several cosmological theories have been developed. This study delves into inherently flat theories within the framework of lattice theory, a concept initially introduced in a 2020 arXiv paper. We examine the proposed lattice-based flatness theories, evaluating their potential to explain the universe's flatness during the cosmic radiation dominance era. A lattice-based approach, however, poses challenges for incorporating particle masses and offers limited opportunities for model modification. Furthermore, even with the incorporation of arbitrary matter and energy variations, some of these models fail to resolve the horizon and flatness problems. A lattice-based flatness theory may only provide an adequate solution when the universe's temperature is above a specific threshold, roughly estimated to be $10^{20}$ Gel'man, a value far exceeding the cosmic radiation dominance era's temperature. A temperature of $10^{20}$ Gel'man corresponds to a time of approximately $10^{-15}$ seconds, a point at which the universe's characteristics are largely unspecified. A rapid change in the universe's temperature is followed by the era of quark-gluon plasma and later big hadronic expansion, where the temperature drops to approximately $10^{12}\sim10^{15}$ GeV, still failing to meet the requirements of the inherently flat lattice-based theories previously evaluated. This study presents a novel variational image partitioning model that integrates techniques from image recovery. The proposed model incorporates a modified Mumford-Shah-like energy with an adapted constraint, facilitating the segmentation of original images adapted from noisy data. By employing the Lagrange multiplier method, we transform the challenge into a conventional Mumford-Shah optimization issue and then apply the prox-Alternating Linearized Minimization (PALM) algorithm to solve the resulting problem. Initially, we test the proposed algorithm on a standard test image and demonstrate its ability to divide this image into distinct regions. Next, we explore various parameters influencing the algorithm's execution and provide a set of qualitative results. Ultimately, we examine the execution time needed to solve the model, specifically under different diffusion coefficients. Interestingly, we find that larger coefficients lead to faster computation times. Finally, we apply the proposed algorithm to a range of noisy images and showcase the resulting segmentations. Notably, the generated segmentations show minimal influence from the noise, indicating the high performance of the proposed model. All of our numerical results illustrate the outstanding capabilities of the proposed algorithm in handling noisy data and demonstrating its potential in image processing. This paper investigates the existence of minimizers and standardizations in the context of a biharmonic Choquard equation, subject to exponential growth constraints. Minimizers are identified as critical points of a related functional, and standardizations are obtained through symmetry-based considerations, yielding a singular metric in the metric theory. Notably, our approach enhances known results from the literature. Due to the lack of coercivity in the functional, compactness is a critical aspect in establishing the existence of minimizers and standardizations, necessitating an initial analysis in an enlarged Sobolev space. Additionally, in the context of exponential growth, we devise a new compactness criterion for bounded subsets in the Sobolev space, enabling the use of a classical Min-Max Theorem to determine the minimizers. Furthermore, we combine the infinite dimensionality of the Sobolev space with a Lagrange multiplier principle to derive the minimizers as local minima of a related constrained functional, and, through a modified Pohozaev identity, demonstrate that the minimizers maintain the required compactness property. Finally, under Taylor growth conditions, we prove the existence of standardizations via a metric theory in conjunction with the metric theorem. Our approach also enables the derivation of asymptotic formulas for the ground state nodes. The content of this paper has been announced in [32]. multi-agent cooperation in human and robot interactions compounds these issues. 
A major obstacle is that existing multi-agent learning approaches are inefficient, 
demanding substantial computational power and limiting their deployment. 
Furthermore, these systems require substantial and often hand-engineered knowledge 
bases, making it difficult to scale up due to the associated high development costs. 
These problems are more acute in applications involving human and robot collaboration. 
This conceptual paper addresses these challenges by exploring the potential of 
utilizing self-organizing artificial life techniques in multi-agent cognitive systems. 
These techniques offer a promising approach to overcoming the knowledge acquisition and 
complexity hurdles, while also addressing the security and trustability issues through 
collective intelligence and decentralized decision-making mechanisms. 
The proposed methodology aims to establish a transparent and reliable foundation for 
large-scale multi-agent cooperative learning between humans and robots. 
This could lead to significant advancements in various applications, such as multi-agent 
education and cooperative robotics.  Key concepts: Multi-agent learning; Artificial life;

Current research uses neural networks to identify these relationships, but they often struggle to capture all relevant information in a text.  To overcome this limitation, a new strategy called RDP is introduced, where the goal is not just to identify textual relationships, but also to predict how these entities are connected in a knowledge graph.  By doing so, the model is forced to consider all entities in the text and thus improves its overall performance.  Experiments conducted on various datasets and tasks demonstrate that RDP consistently outperforms existing models in relation discovery, outperforming them by a significant margin.  Additionally, the model's ability to capture long-distance relationships in a text has been proven, with the model achieving state-of-the-art results on various datasets.  Further analysis shows that the model is capable of considering multiple relationships in a text and that its components work in unison to provide a comprehensive understanding of the text's meaning.  Finally, the model's code and datasets have been made publicly available for other researchers to access.  When tested on a zero-shot setting, the model demonstrated its ability to understand and make connections in knowledge graphs, even when only provided with texts that do not contain all the entities in the graph. All in consideration, the model provides a significant improvement over existing solutions in relation discovery.  The model's performance can be attributed to its ability to capture long-distance relationships and its ability to understand and predict connections in knowledge graphs. We explore a novel paradigm for deep learning, which we call the 'Functional Dilemma' to represent the inherent challenges of deep learning architectures. The depth of a neural network is measured not just by its number of layers but also by its handling of distinct data types and modes. We identify two key components: a binder that combines input data with a weight matrix, and a recorder that transforms the bound data into output form. With this framework, we examine various convolutional neural network configurations and their applications to 2D image and 3D medical image analysis, ultimately leading to the development of a general deep learning architecture called the OmniNet. By adapting this model, we demonstrate the feasibility of applying deep learning to challenging 3D medical image processing tasks. We also introduce a new device called the OmniCom, a deep learning-based data compressor that can restore original input data from its transformed form with high accuracy. We showcase the effectiveness of this data compressor on a range of 3D medical image restoration tasks. Throughout the paper, we emphasize the importance of theoretical results to inform the design and development of deep learning models. With this research, we aim to contribute to the foundational understanding of deep learning, which we believe is essential for further advancements in this area. Nobuki had previously defined the depth of an element in a monoid as its smallest possible upper bound among which it could be a zero divisor. In this study, we expand upon Nobuki's concept of depth within monoids by introducing the idea of a chief element and demonstrating its significance through its connection to lattice points in a monoid. Specifically, we show that in a finitely generated monoid, an element is a chief element if and only if it reaches the maximum possible lattice depth within the monoid. Additionally, we present a method for determining the depth of an arbitrary chief element in a finitely generated monoid. In the course of this work, we also establish a key relationship between zero sets and prime ideals in a monoid and its corresponding upper monoid ideal lattice, which may be of independent interest. We further provide a detailed analysis of chief elements within upper nilmonoids, revealing that an element is a chief element if and only if it consists of a product of square-free components that use each prime divisor at most once. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of chief elements within upper nilmonoids that are not nilpotent. We also investigate when an element that is a chief generator in a monoid also constitutes a chief element, showing that this condition is satisfied if the monoid is commutative or has a specific free product structure. Finally, we examine the relationship between lattice points and chief elements within upper nilmonoids, revealing that an element is a lattice point if and only if it is a chief element with a specific additional property. A major issue with deep neural networks applying to quantum many-body problems lies in the sign problem that arises when representing fermionic particles with complex numbers. The sign problem necessitates an extensive optimization of the network parameters to minimize the overall sign, a challenging task in many contexts. Here, in the framework of lattice quantum Monte Carlo methods, we introduce a new type of neural network called the CFSNN, capable of directly handling the complex signs associated with fermionic particles. The CFSNN incorporates an inherent phase factor in its definition, thereby eliminating the need for extensive optimization of the network parameters to account for the sign problem. Consequently, this breakthrough results in a considerable reduction in the computational cost required to achieve a satisfactory approximation. We substantiate the performance of the CFSNN by applying it to a traditional test case, the ground state phase transition in the t-J model on a 2D square lattice, and find it to be in agreement with existing literature and contemporary sign-based methods. Due to its effectiveness in handling the sign problem, the CFSNN has the potential to significantly streamline calculations in various quantum many-body systems. The code used to generate the results in this study is publicly accessible via the public GitHub repository: https://github.com/cfneuralnetwork/CFSNN.git. Additionally, the results of the calculations mentioned in this research are available on the public arXiv repository: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06564. Lastly, the reference for the work by Pruitt et al. that the research by our group is based on is given by B. D. Pruitt, S. Kowalski, and S. Kunkel, Phys. Rev. B 98 (18), 180201 (2018). This work is also publicly accessible at the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09091. In contrast to Pruitt et al.'s conclusions regarding the feasibility of neural networks to tackle the sign problem, our results indicate that the CFSNN holds considerable promise in addressing this issue. A well-known issue in the Standard Model of particle physics is the known charge disparity among different quarks and leptons. This problem, known as quark-lepton duality, can be addressed through the introduction of flavour-breaking Flavon-Higgs fields, which can also account for the emergence of small neutrino masses. Given that explicit flavour violation is heavily constrained by experimental data, any potential Flavon model must incorporate a rigorous flavour symmetry. The possibility of discovering the Flavon at upcoming colliders, like HL-LHC or future lepton or hadron colliders, is a feasible prospect. The potential signatures of Flavon production, such as long-lived particles or ones that decay into Higgs bosons, are examined in depth. The evaluation of this process's effectiveness for detecting the Flavon at future colliders, like a 100 TeV hadron collider or a 27 TeV muon collider, is a key aspect of this research. The potential for lepton or hadron colliders to identify the Flavon by observing its influence on charged leptons is also analyzed. The possible outcomes of discovering the Flavon or its complementary states, as well as the potential breakthroughs in understanding flavour physics that may result from these discoveries, are explored. Finally, the potential for the Flavon or its counterparts to mediate the decay of the top quark and Higgs boson is examined in detail. The potential for this process at future colliders, such as HL-LHC or 100 TeV hadron collider, to verify the Flavon or its counterparts is analyzed. The evaluation includes a thorough assessment of the statistical and systematic uncertainties associated with this process. The potential for this process to verify the Flavon or its counterparts at future colliders, such as 27 TeV muon collider, is also examined. The potential outcomes of verifying the Flavon or its counterparts, as well as the potential breakthroughs in understanding flavour physics that may result from these discoveries, are explored. The study also includes a comprehensive comparison with the predictions of minimal R-parity violating supersymmetry. The outcome of this comparison reveals that the detection of the Flavon or its counterparts provides stronger constraints on flavour-changing neutral currents than the LHC can achieve. Our understanding of how people perceive and interact with their environment is fundamental to how we experience reality. Advances in (semi)-autarkic sensing and communication technologies like VR have brought about a new dimension of interaction, allowing direct access to digital information. This novel form of interaction raises interesting research questions about how people perceive and interact with it. This study explores the aspect of shadow perception in VR, examining participants' ability to recognize and differentiate between real and digitally created shadows. The results show that VR shadows are consistently distinguished from real ones, and the level of accuracy in identifying VR shadows remains stable across different ages. Notably, the study found that participants were also able to identify artificially created shadows in real scenes, suggesting that the way software generates shadows can be discernible from real ones. The study's findings have implications for the use of shadow perception in social VR environments and the design of more realistic interactions. The research outcomes can contribute to the development of more immersive and interactive experiences in social VR settings. Future research can utilize these findings to create more realistic and interactive worlds, enhancing user engagement and empathy in social VR environments. To assess the suitability of various neural language processing architectures for processing less commonly studied languages, we adapt the BigScience multilingual language model to three under-studied tongues: Khmer, Mongolian, and Nepali. Our model, fine-tuned on a 404-million word dataset, achieves notable success in zero-shot settings, particularly in Khmer and Nepali, using an analysis of automatic evaluation metrics. Nonetheless, it falls short in understanding language-specific nuances in Mongolian. In further exploration, we discover that the performance of our models in zero-shot settings heavily relies on the quality of available training data and that automatic evaluation metrics often contradict human judgments. Ultimately, we suggest that models from both the T5 and FLAME architectures remain susceptible to biases from their underlying multilingual training datasets. Lastly, we emphasize the importance of diverse representation in shaping the future development of NLP frameworks. This research introduces the M-ar-K-Fast version of the Adaptive Rank-based Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (ArKCCA) algorithm, specifically designed for large-scale mixed-type data sets. Canicular components are generated using a novel, efficient approach based on working with individual Gaussian distributions instead of integrating the kernel and adaptation techniques. This method is further enhanced by adding sparsity and autonomy components, which utilize the L1-SCAD penalty to select relevant features and maximize autonomy through stochastic optimization. The resulting sparsity and autonomy canicular components provide a comprehensive understanding of complex data sets. Experimental evaluations using real-world data sets confirm the superior performance of the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm in both feature construction and model selection across various configurations and dimensions. Additionally, the study demonstrates the computational efficiency of the model, enabling it to process high-dimensional data effectively. The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm is an improved implementation of the ArKCCA method, exhibiting enhanced performance and capabilities. The primary objective is to identify a suitable framework that enables a precise translation of verifiable cryptographic protocols in relation to assertions of impossibility, particularly those involving undecidable properties. Specifically, IML is better equipped to express undecidable properties within a framework of minimal assumptions, thereby facilitating a more straightforward translation of verifiable cryptographic protocols. Moreover, IML's ability to facilitate a direct comparison between assertions of impossibility and their negations, known as dualities, proves particularly useful in this regard. including spatially referenced posts that enable real-time monitoring of evolving situations.
However, current approaches to event identification on social media are largely limited to
text-based analysis, overlooking the significance of spatial context.

text analysis with geographic proximity analysis, allowing multiple events to occur at
the same location, as observed in real-world scenarios, such as concerts and road closures.

identifying 87.65% of recognized events, including the primary spatial-temporal event and
associated sub-events. The associated video presents an illustrative example of event
identification, highlighting the importance of combining text and spatial analysis. The source code

A new framework aims to bridge this gap by developing Bayesian methods that can both withstand and recognize attacks from a trusted pool of sources. The framework's first challenge is to establish a metric that quantifies the likelihood of an estimation source being compromised, and to create a prior distribution that reflects this risk. The second challenge is to derive a posterior distribution that takes into account the probability of compromise given the observation. The third challenge is to design an efficient computational method that can handle complex distributions. The framework is applied to two scenarios: scaling measurement units and estimating a vector benchmark, and first-rate experimental results show that it successfully detects and resists attacks with minimal disruption to conventional estimation outcomes. In early 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic spread across China, causing the government to implement strict digital control measures. These moves led to an increase in state-sponsored digital propaganda, aiming to counteract malicious digital information. This study analyzes the spread of official digital rumors within China, particularly in the critical period following the pandemic's outbreak. Our research highlights the role of a spreading mechanism within China's environment, contrasting with the anti-symmetric pattern typically seen in social media networks. We also examine the effects of the pandemic on digital information dissemination, focusing on factors such as time, geographic location, and topics. Our findings show that counter-measures like the blocking of specific websites and topics did not significantly influence the spread of digital rumors, while also revealing patterns of synchronized spreading across different social media platforms. Ultimately, this study seeks to contribute to the understanding of digital information dissemination in environments with heavy digital control, drawing comparisons to the unique circumstances of China during the pandemic. Our work may also yield insights for applications such as digital counter-measures, influence maximization, and online risk control in environments with characteristics similar to those of China during the pandemic. Due to its exclusivity, our research on China is likely to be relevant to investigations of other heavily digitally controlled environments. Recent breakthroughs in multiple natural language frameworks have occurred almost a decade apart from each other, with some attributes common to all of them, such as using continuous representations and compositional structures. This study reveals that frameworks are drawn to a limited number of concepts, and we identify five core ideas - semantic modules, type of context used, direction of meaning transfer, degree of context inclusion, and level of context specificity - which define the reduction criteria for natural language frameworks. By applying these criteria, we map the development of natural language frameworks in sequence and find patterns in the progression, including frequent combinations of the concepts and unexpected separations of the concepts. This leads to new insights and potential avenues for further research. The reduction criteria we established can be used to construct natural language frameworks quickly and efficiently, and we demonstrate this by building a new framework, DepCom, in just a few weeks. DepCom outperforms previous frameworks and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple evaluation measures. The main concept guiding DepCom's design is the layered structure of contexts, which may be applied to other frameworks to improve their performance. The choice of loss function for a deep neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions and classification problems that exist. Current knowledge primarily emphasizes the effectiveness of different loss functions, often derived from theoretical considerations, without investigating their combined effects on classification performance. In this study, a comprehensive analysis on multiple datasets was conducted to explore the impact of altering loss functions on deep neural networks. The results demonstrated that, in addition to influencing classification outcomes, varying loss functions also affected the resulting model parameters, resulting in distinct feature representations and classification results. The optimality of a deep neural network model depends on an optimal combination of accuracy and other evaluation metrics, rather than solely on the best possible accuracy, as previously considered. Therefore, a more comprehensive approach is required to search for the optimal loss function, as suggested by our method of simultaneous training of multiple models, leading to better overall performance and a greater understanding of the network's internal workings. The proposed method also facilitates the generation of different models from a single pre-trained neural network, thus enabling the creation of a family of suitable models for a given task through a simple transformation of the original model. Our research, powered by extensive parallel computing capabilities, provides valuable insights into the relationship between loss functions and classification performance, ultimately paving the way for a more nuanced understanding of the functioning of deep neural networks. In the US, law enforcement and the general public have an ongoing discussion about police transparency and accountability. One of the key challenges is the lack of publicly available and transparent information about police activities, making it difficult to understand what they do and how they interact with the community. Current systems have limitations in that they often rely on already-incidents-based interfaces, ignoring the valuable insights provided by users during dispatching calls and subsequent engagements with emergency services. This paper explores the potential of text-based reporting systems in revealing concealed user-dispatcher engagements through analytical techniques. By applying these methods, emergency call centers can gain valuable knowledge, enhancing their services and ultimately improving public safety. Three analytical tools were developed and tested on a full year's worth of real-life calls from a large US call center, demonstrating the extraction of over 3500 engagements from over 1500 hours of calls. Our findings illustrate the diverse nature of engagements, their frequent occurrence, and the importance of enhanced dispatcher-user interactions. Moreover, the developed system facilitated the automatic identification of engagements in a center with a high volume of calls, necessitating further training to achieve optimal performance in other centers. This research provides a foundation for future investigations in using text-based reporting systems to understand and improve police-dispatcher-public interactions. Additionally, two illustrative examples show how the extracted engagements can inform strategies to strengthen relationships between emergency responders and the general public. This study offers a comprehensive framework that can be adapted by other research communities and emergency services to improve their understanding and engagement with the community, ultimately leading to better public safety services. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on a novel type of hybrid superconductor that combines electric and magnetic properties, we computationally simulate how its magnetic moments respond to applied magnetization. Under these conditions, we found that the magnetic moments are attracted to the applied magnetization in a region where superconductivity is present, specifically within a critical area near the applied magnetization's direction. This attractive interaction increases as the applied magnetization's strength increases, particularly when its direction aligns with the applied field. In a scenario where the applied magnetization is not aligned with superconducting direction, we observed a decrease in magnetic moments and an increase in their susceptibility, especially at low temperatures. This behavior is reminiscent of the classic "Pauli paramagnetism" observed in certain alloys and can be caused by the unpaired spins within the superconductor that are not effectively paired. Furthermore, we found that the applied magnetization's impact is most pronounced at its boundary and at a specific layer within the superconductor. This boundary layer exhibits unique physical properties that differ from the rest of the superconductor and is known to behave uniquely under applied magnetization. As a result, we propose that the applied magnetization's interaction with the superconductor is mediated by a triplet Cooper pair's unique magnetic properties and the superconductor's novel magnetic structure. In particular, we studied a specific type of superconductor called SrNCLnO ($\mathrm{Ln} = \mathrm{Eu}$, $\mathrm{Gd}$) with a specific layered structure, where we found that the applied magnetization's impact is most pronounced at its boundary and at a specific layer within the superconductor. Finally, we studied the potential magnetic structures of the superconductor and observed that the applied magnetization's interaction is most pronounced in a structure that has a net magnetic moment while preserving its superconducting properties. However, this does not hold for other structures that have no net magnetic moment. As a result, we found that the applied magnetization's interaction is not sufficient to explain a long-theorized phenomenon where a normal, non-magnetic material exhibits magnetic properties in a cavity with applied magnetization. Nevertheless, we computed the applied magnetization's effect on superconducting properties and observed that it exhibits unique, temperature-dependent behavior. In particular, we found that the applied magnetization's effect on superconducting gap is not uniform within the material and that it is most pronounced at a certain layer within the superconductor and at its boundary.

In the past few decades, the way data is structured within musical recordings has undergone significant changes. To quantify this transformation, researchers have proposed using data complexity measures, such as Pearson correlation information and random Fourier features, to evaluate how audio is represented. However, these methods often require large datasets to produce reliable results, but are also prone to false positives when working with small datasets. To address this issue, this study introduces a novel approach to assessing the complexity of compact discs based on the spatial distribution of audio features. By applying this method to a collection of selected albums spanning the period 1970-2010, the results show a notable increase in complexity around the year 2000. Furthermore, a simplified model is also presented that seeks to identify the underlying causes of this shift in musical recording structure. Overall, this work aims to contribute to the development of more efficient methods for analysing the evolution of musical data complexity. To facilitate future research, the source code and datasets used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/jbarchichon/evolucy/tree/main. This work is an extension of the authors' previous investigation into the temporal evolution of data complexity in popular Western music, published in a conference paper in 2021. Significant advancements have led to the development of new methods and results presented here. In particular, the novel approach to measuring data complexity has been validated through extensive testing on various datasets, and its accuracy is compared to that of Pearson correlation information and random Fourier features. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method is a more effective tool for analysing the change in musical data complexity over time. Additionally, this study delves into the theoretical aspects of using this new approach to measure data complexity and incorporates it into a stochastic model that seeks to explain the increase in complexity recorded on compact discs since the year 2000. To verify the findings and evaluate the performance of the proposed method, numerous experiments were conducted using various datasets of musical recordings. These experiments compare the results of three different complexity measures - spatial, Pearson correlation information, and random Fourier features - on datasets of different sizes to examine their convergence and accuracy in predicting the data complexity of given recordings. The results show that the proposed spatial method consistently produces accurate predictions of data complexity, particularly when working with small datasets. Moreover, this study investigates the relationship between data complexity and other characteristics, such as audio features and genre labels, using techniques from machine learning and information theory. The results reveal connections between data complexity and the distribution of audio features and genre labels in musical recordings.

Our novel approach for reward learning in complex decision-making scenarios utilizes visually assisted cluster evaluation to rapidly and efficiently identify relevant experiences among a vast state space. By leveraging this experience selection method, the training process is streamlined and completed significantly faster. The chosen experiences are then used to enhance a target policy through offline learning, effectively optimizing it and overcoming the limitations of traditional offline reinforcement learning techniques that often suffer from biased experience selection towards regions of high visitation, rather than high potential reward. By visually supporting the ranking of experiences, our method successfully overcomes the challenges of reward learning by significantly reducing the time required to complete the training process while simultaneously improving the quality of the generated policies. For instance, on the Ford Bobby test case, our approach reduces the offline training time for Ford Bobby by three orders of magnitude while achieving a Tsai score of 0.814, surpassing Ford Bobby's baseline score of 0.176. Additional experimental evaluations, incorporating the scenarios of Classic Control and Grid Landscapes, also demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in prioritizing high-potential reward experiences and enhancing the quality of the generated policies. Crucially, the success of our method relies on cluster formation and experience selection that prioritizes high-potential reward regions of the state space with the support of visual tools, rather than simply experiencing the state most frequently visited. In contrast to existing reinforcement learning techniques that either ignore visual data or use it to direct exploration, our approach successfully integrates visual data with experience selection to improve the quality of the generated policies. By facilitating the efficient selection of experiences, our approach bridges the gap between the Markov and non-Markov domains of the task and enables the training of high-quality policies. Furthermore, the success of our method in prioritizing high-potential reward experiences lays the foundation for additional applications of visual data in reinforcement learning. Emerging from this research, the concept of visually assisted cluster evaluation has far-reaching implications for reward learning and machine learning in general, empowering the efficient selection of experiences in various scenarios. Furthermore, we establish that this property can be expressed through the use of a particular topology known as the Scott topology. Our work builds upon a prior discovery regarding the Scott topology on the Smyth powerspace, where it was shown to be a compatible extension of the original Scott topology. The core-conciseness property can be seen as a topological manifestation of a concept initially introduced in the field of modal logic, particularly in the study of bisimilarity. A new approach, known as Standardized Enhanced Inverse Likelihood Weighting (SEILW), is developed as a simple and effective extension of the EW (Exponential Weighting) family to handle censored data under a continuous distribution, like Gaussian distribution. SEILW is essentially an optimization of the standard EWEM (Exponential Weighting for Expected Shortfalls) objective function by replacing the loss function with a more sensitive form that takes into account outcomes below threshold as well as losses above thresholds proportionally. This modification has the benefit of simplifying the complex derivative of EWEM by turning it into a tractable standard objective function that can be efficiently calculated. By applying this change, SEILW emerges as a straightforward standardization of EWEM, yielding better results and fewer occurrences of extreme overweighting in low probability events. Furthermore, SEILW is combined with NN (Neural Network) forecasts to create SEILW-NN, allowing both models to benefit from each other's strengths. By integrating these models, the loss in accuracy due to censored losses on low probability events is compensated for by the improved loss calculation of SEILW-NN. Experimental findings demonstrate that SEILW-NN surpasses both SEILW and NN models in loss calculation, while also outperforming them in model accuracy. A study involving loss under specific threshold scenarios confirms that SEILW-NN successfully mitigates the issue of extreme overweighting in low probability events. Lastly, the proposed SEILW-NN is applied to a real-world scenario to verify its effectiveness compared to the alternative model, EWEM-NN. A comparison of the loss calculation from both models shows that SEILW-NN achieves lower values than EWEM-NN. To verify that the observed differences between the models were not due to chance, a hypothesis test was conducted and the results indicate that SEILW-NN significantly outperforms EWEM-NN. Based on these results, the development of SEILW-NN is a significant advancement in loss calculation model design. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it also means that parameter estimation is subject to bias. We develop and investigate new unbiased minimum variance estimators for the parameters of the Poisson process, specifically those of the ultimate quantile and the average excess, in the case where extreme event times are recorded. These estimators are based on a reparameterization of the original model and are shown to have certain optimal properties. Our results are verified through simulations and applications to real-data sets. Additionally, we present a novel method for assessing the reliability of extreme value estimates, specifically the amounts by which their accuracy falls short of being optimal. This methodology could be adapted to other types of estimators and can serve as a benchmark for evaluating their performance. Lastly, we explore the properties of the estimators when used in conjunction with other estimation methods. To our knowledge, this is a contribution to the field of extreme value theory that had not been previously investigated. We propose a theory to explain the origin of millisecond pulsars (MSPs) by assuming their gaseous cores transform into dwarfs at an advanced stage of star evolution. We then investigate the parameters of MSP formation by analyzing the masses of these dwarfs. By utilizing the advanced self-consistent calculations of white dwarf structures, we demonstrate that 1) the gaseous core formation in massive stars at an advanced stage of evolution leads to MSPs with characteristic spin periods and magnetic fields; 2) the masses of these cores, MSP-progenitor stars, and MSPs themselves, are closely related and fall within a specific range; 3) MSP formation via core collapse in supergiant stars would result in unusual mass distributions; 4) the core masses of dwarfs and MSPs, derived from analysis of their mass relationships, are in agreement with each other and provide crucial insights into the pale dwarfs' (pre-pulsar star) structure and the MSP formation mechanism. This novel approach offers an innovative solution to long-standing puzzles surrounding MSP origins, as well as new perspectives on pulsar theory and star evolution, and lays the foundation for an original research area focused on the utilization of advanced mesh-free methods in star and neutron star studies. Additionally, we introduce mesh-free Alvar-Einstein-Collins (AIC) method, which we utilize to compute white dwarf structures and perform mass analysis through an automatic process. This integration of AIC and mesh-free techniques enables the acceleration of computations by a factor of 5 compared to traditional finite-volume methods. Additionally, we outline potential future modifications to our theory to incorporate recent developments in mesh-free variants of the Einstein field equations, as well as the utilization of our model in various applications, such as nuclear double beta decay and neutron star mergers. This way, we bridge pulsar theory and mesh-free computational methods, by examining common origins and outcomes, and enabling high-performance computing of various spectral and source analysis problems. Our work is characterized by a unique blend of theoretical and computational insights, obtained through an automatic process. In this research, we introduce a novel approach called GANDOR, which breaks down DNNs into more interpretable models composed of simple logical rules. Unlike other methods, GANDOR doesn't limit these rules to input and output correlations, but rather captures complex logical concepts within the model's internal representations. By employing concept analysis and using Inverse Method Reconstruction, GANDOR identifies these concepts and generates more comprehensive explanations for DNN predictions. Concept analysis enables the study of complex high-level concepts in machine learning, particularly those involving inclusion and segregation principles, without requiring additional parameters. This powerful tool has far-reaching applications in various fields, and our work with GANDOR represents a significant advancement in the field. In experiments on 8 datasets, GANDOR outperformed existing methods in generating clarifications that are more detailed, accurate, and consistent with the model's internal representations. Additionally, GANDOR's performance scaled better than other approaches with an increase in dataset size. Our findings are a promising sign that clarifications can learn to represent complex concepts effectively, even in challenging scenarios. To facilitate this, GANDOR's concept discovery and generation processes were designed with efficiency in mind, and our results from 3 case studies demonstrate that GANDOR's findings are also adopted by other state-of-the-art explanation methods. Our research offers several opportunities for future growth, and we explored one potential avenue by extending GANDOR to work with attention-based DNNs. In these experiments, GANDOR's performance improved significantly, reaching new heights in terms of clarity and completeness of its generated clarifications. This result suggests that incorporating attention mechanisms into GANDOR is a beneficial modification. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a popular choice for addresssing natural language processing challenges, particularly for sentiment classification tasks. However, they face a critical issue of over-blurring, which occurs when they fail to capture precise task-specific information from the input graph. Specifically, GCNs suffer from over-blurring when they combine nodes with significantly different semantic meanings. To address this limitation, we develop a novel over-blurring mitigation approach for GCNs, which prioritizes retaining task-relevant information. Our method comprises two key components: (1) a semantic relevance calculator that assesses node significance, and (2) a linear transformer-based GCN (LT-GCN) that reduces over-blurring by focusing on critical nodes. Our findings show that LT-GCN outperforms existing state-of-the-art models and remains computationally efficient. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark consisting of three datasets to evaluate over-blurring in GCNs. Our research offers insights into addressing the over-blurring issue in GCNs, which can be applied to other graph neural networks as well. The proposed method and benchmark are open-source and can be accessed at https://github.com/jbmeke/Overblur-GCNs. Experimental evidence and the source code are available at this site. Research into transition metal alloys, like Heusler layers, has gained significant interest due to their exceptional magnetic and electrical properties. Current methods for growing these alloys, such as epitaxial techniques, face several limitations. In this study, we investigated the epitaxial growth of Heusler layers, specifically R2M2X4 (RM=Co,Ni; RMX=Sn,Sb), using a unique substrate configuration consisting of graphene on sapphire. This configuration offers multiple epitaxial methods as an alternative to traditional techniques, like van der Waals epitaxy. By fine-tuning kinetic parameters during molecular beam epitaxy, we achieved multiple equilibrium solutions, including distant epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, and van der Waals epitaxy. Our findings indicate that adjusting epitaxial van der Waals layer thickness and kinetic particle flux can switch Heusler layers' epitaxial configuration. This enables a new method of controlling epitaxial growth through rational particle flux optimization. Leveraging a detailed analytical model, we understood the underlying mechanisms of this technique and demonstrated the possibility of achieving single domain epitaxy through this method. Our work presents a groundbreaking approach to controlling epitaxial growth, offering new possibilities for growing high-quality transition metal alloys. Additionally, this technique has potential applications beyond Heusler layers and could be used to develop other materials with unique magnetic and electrical properties. With further research, this method can be used to develop innovative, multi-functional devices in fields like spintronics, topological computing, and quantum technology. Given its potential applications, we regrouped the results to clarify the connections between kinetic particle flux, epitaxial configuration, and magnetic/ electrical properties, enabling readers to quickly understand the relationships between these key factors. Furthermore, we explored the efficiency of this growth technique, comparing its results to those obtained with other techniques, like Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis confirmed that this kinetic parameter control offers several advantages over other distribution methods, ultimately enabling the development of high-quality transition metal alloys with optimized magnetic and electrical properties, as well as increased efficiency and lower particle flux requirements. These findings could pave the way for implementing this kinetic parameter control in real-world manufacturing processes to produce large quantities of these materials. Lastly, we extended our analytical model to investigate the mechanism of this kinetic parameter control in three-dimensional systems, enabling us to maintain lateral composition homogeneity during epitaxial growth. Our analysis confirmed that this kinetic parameter control enables not only single domain epitaxy but also three-dimensional single domain epitaxy in specific cases

This study develops an advanced heart sound classification system designed to adapt to these variations. Unlike existing methods, our system acknowledges the dynamic nature of heart sounds and incorporates the principle of superposition, addressing both internal changes and external distractions. Internally, our model accounts for the heart's increased contraction force due to heightened nervous stimulation, causing normal heart sounds to modulate their frequency content. Externally, our system considers the superposition of heart sounds by incorporating time-shifted copies of the template signals, effectively mitigating the impact of overlapping sounds. Convolutional Neural Networks are applied to the modulated frequency spectra, followed by a simple decision-making process using the softmax function. This proposed system is tested on a database comprising 1000 heart sounds, demonstrating a high accuracy rate of 87.9% without any pre-processing. Our research showcases a successful approach to analyzing heart sounds with intrinsic variability and highlights the benefits of incorporating the superposition principle in signal processing. Additionally, our study points out the possibility of using deep learning methods to solve classification problems involving complex, variable signals such as those produced by heart function at rest and during physical activity. The Auction Design Theory proposes the Second-Price Auction as an efficient mechanism for obtaining truthful bids. We conducted an empirical study to test if bidders truthfully report their values in such auctions, specifically examining the impact of bidding strategies and information availability on auction outcomes. Our results align with theory when bidders only base their bids on the minimum required to win and rank other bidders' values; however, when strategizing goes beyond this basic requirement, both truthful and non-truthful bidding strategies emerge. When bidders share the same value distribution and rank their preferences similarly, but their actual values vary, we observed an increase in detected misrepresentation. Furthermore, bidding strategies were more frequently employed when bidders shared similar value distributions and ranks, leading to reduced truthfulness. These findings indicate a critical assumption underlies the efficiency of trustless Second-Price Auctions - where bidders only bid the minimum required to win and rank other bidders' values equally - is often violated. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition with fundamental symptoms of inattention, excessive activity, and impulsiveness. The nature of ADHD is complex and involves multi-regional brain activity, making ADHD diagnosis challenging based on clinical evaluation alone. The emergence of neuroimaging technologies, particularly resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), has significantly improved understanding and diagnosing ADHD. Recent studies exploit rs-fMRI combined with machine learning to improve ADHD diagnosis, but this approach faces difficulties in differentiating individuals due to the model's reliance on a large number of trained parameters and intricate network connections. To address this issue, this study aims to enhance ADHD diagnosis accuracy through data-driven and feature-extraction methods by selecting crucial regions of the brain for analysis. The proposed dataset and framework comprise rs-fMRI image acquisition, preprocessing, feature selection, model training, and testing. The novel contribution of this study centers around identifying essential regions for enhanced ADHD diagnosis, whereas conventional methods utilize the entire brain for diagnosis. The selected regions are based on discrete time series features extracted from rs-fMRI data, specifically wavelet energy features, which distinguish ADHD and HC groups. The proposed research outperforms existing literature in ADHD diagnosis accuracy when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study investigates the brain regions of significance in ADHD diagnosis and explores potential future studies on characterizing ADHD alterations through connectivity patterns between these critical regions. The study validates its enhancements against existing literature on ADHD diagnosis via rs-fMRI data. The proposed algorithm is trained, tested, and validated using leave-one-out CV due to its sufficient data availability. The study demonstrates improvements in diagnosis accuracy, entropymetric measures, and HC classification in three datasets (IAC, ADHD200, and combined IAC+ADHD200). The study is original and contributes to the field of ADHD diagnosis via rs-fMRI data in various ways. The obtained results are consistent and generalizable to other datasets. Current DNA storage systems, such as DNAdrive and Archive, utilize a flat organization where all files are equally accessible and fetched equally, leading to poor get-best performance, especially when retrieving multiple related files. Additionally, when updating DNA archives due to file modifications, the entire modified segment must be re-synthesized from the old version, leading to inefficient utilization of the old data. Our proposed system, Hierarchical DNA Storage (HDS), structures DNA archives in a nested, hierarchical format for optimal get-best performance, and enhances storage efficiency by allowing specified files to be updated without re-synthesizing entire segments. HDS achieves higher get-best and utilization benchmarks than competing systems. For example, when testing with 16 related files, HDS achieves a 30.96% improvement in get-best and a 67.19% improvement in utilization over DNAdrive. Our experimental results also demonstrate the feasibility of HDS with a 12.52% improvement in get-best and a 48.19% improvement in utilization over Archive, even when incorporating higher costs. HDS's major components, such as hierarchical file organization, multi-level file fetching, and segment updating, are all open-source software solutions. Our experiments also validate the performance of our custom DNA sequence conversion tool, FastDCS. In an array of phase oscillators, as diversity among the oscillators' frequencies and time constants increases, the dynamics shift from a conserved pattern of local synchronization to a non-local synchronization pattern, potentially leading to errors in time series analysis. Furthermore, local synchronization in interconnected oscillators may also suffer from these diversity effects. We've investigated the phase dynamics of an array of diverse oscillators, either linearly or non-linearly coupled, and found that local synchronization in interconnected oscillators tends to local temporal stability, regardless of the type of non-linear coupling and frequency dispersion. However, the phase dynamics in arrays with non-linear interactions is more complex, as it doesn't follow the widely accepted Kuramoto model's predictions, especially in large diversity cases with negative global coupling. Interestingly, local stability in arrays of linearly coupled oscillators is influenced by the balance between the square of global coupling and diversity in the limit of large sizes. Moreover, the non-linearly coupled system's stability in large sizes is influenced by the global coupling being larger than a certain threshold, regardless of the extent of diversity. We've also explored the applicability and limitations of the mean-field approximation in large sizes for both linear and non-linear coupled systems. The diversity-driven changes in the stable local synchronization pattern from small global coupling to large global coupling were confirmed through numerical solutions and time-series data analysis of diverse biological systems. Finally, we've suggested other research areas that could benefit from these findings, such as the analysis of phase-amplitude dynamics in diverse oscillator arrays. The proposed model for describing the local synchronization in arrays of diverse oscillator arrays could have various practical applications, such as designing coordinated clock networks and developing algorithms for detecting local errors in clock signals. The study also opens up possibilities for exploring other diverse oscillator arrays from a theoretical perspective. The work further highlights the need to consider the phase history of interacting components (with different time constants) when analyzing the local synchronization in arrays of diverse oscillator arrays. The result also has implications for designing local synchronization in diverse oscillator arrays, such as implementing local feedback mechanisms to maintain local synchronization in arrays with negative global coupling. The study also reveals the limitations of the mean-field approximation in large sizes for both linear and non-linear coupled systems and suggests other research areas, such as exploring the diversity-dependent corrections to the local synchronization in arrays of diverse oscillator arrays with negative global coupling. Our investigation focuses on the stability of dark solitons in the mean-field BEC and Gross-Pitaevskii equations, taking into account the non-linear intensity-dependent dispersion effect. It's observed that for negative dispersion, small initial disturbances can lead to soliton collapse. Contrarily, for positive dispersion, large initial disturbances are more likely to result in soliton collapse. A detailed analysis, involving numerical examples and mathematical theory, reveals that for both scenarios, there are specific thresholds for initial disturbance sizes, wherein the soliton neither collapses nor remains stationary. Moreover, it's discovered through numerical calculations that the collision of two dark solitons in the BEC context leads to a $2\to 2$ scattering outcome. Implications of these findings for real-world optical experiments, particularly in the context of unstable dark spatial solitons, are explored. It's also noted that achieving the required scale of wavefront distortion for observing soliton collapse in experiments poses a significant challenge. For optical applications, it's usually not possible to produce such large distortion scales. Consequently, it's Anticipated that soliton collapse will primarily be of theoretical interest rather than a practical concern in optical systems. Nonetheless, this phenomenon may contribute to the development of novel optical systems, such as dark optical waveguides, that exploit soliton collapse to facilitate the self-trapping of light. Furthermore, it's noted that the occurrence of soliton collapse may be avoided in experiments using light, particularly when using focusing instead of defocusing non-linearity, thereby yielding stable dark solitons. The flow of heat through a stationary bed of spheres is being studied by comparing computational models with experimental data obtained using rapid Magnetic Resonance Imaging. This imaging technique enabled us to observe the temperature distribution within a bed of glass beads filled with water, at varying mean flow velocities ranging from 0 to 1.13 m/s. When scientists evaluate the performance of multiple algorithms for a specific computational challenge, like ranking them on a leaderboard, each algorithm's "type-A" uncertainty - its own variability - can create significant obstacles in making informed comparisons. In the context of evolutionary algorithm research, this issue is particularly prevalent due to the numerous available variants and hyperparameters that significantly affect their behavior. Consequently, identifying the most suitable hyperparameters becomes a critical task, but current studies are hindered by the limitations of small sample sizes and narrow samples. 

To tackle these challenges, we propose employing global sensitivity methods from risk assessment to assess how sensitive evolutionary algorithm outcomes are to their design choices and to utilize these results to identify the most influential hyperparameters in the sample size range that we are working within. This approach, grounded in reliability engineering, helps researchers to (1) prioritize further investigations into the most impactful hyperparameters, (2) develop strategies to reduce their associated uncertainty as quickly as possible, and (3) effectively present results in a way that takes into account the impact of their choices. This general framework is then illustrated with applications to two practical problems: tuning the parameters of these algorithms to find the optimal solution and comparing their performance on a specific task. This study introduces a novel application of global sensitivity analysis to the evaluation of algorithmic hyperparameters and provides open-source implementation of the described techniques. Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture is a significant hypothesis in additive combinatorics that has far-reaching implications. It asserts that if two subsets A and B of an abelian group G have a substantial intersection and a near-additive overlap, then they must be markedly similar in structure. Specifically, for any given δ > 0, if A and B have sizes of at least 3k and 4k respectively, and their intersection consists of at least 1k elements, then there exist two subset sums from A and B that coincide and whose combined size exceeds 5k, thereby indicating a close relationship between the two subsets.

Our research aims to demonstrate that the minimum size requirement for the intersection of A and B can be reduced from 1k to (3/2 - δ)k for any given δ > 0. In particular, for δ = 0.1, this means the intersection needs to consist of at least 2.5k elements to prove the 3k-4 conjecture. Our approach to this problem involves a combination of the Erdős Sumset Theorem, a generalized iterated Cauchy-Davenport theorem, and a novel partitioning scheme designed to analyze additive structures within groups of large size. In addition, our method enables the complete resolution of Freiman's 4k-5 conjecture. Although our result is still short of the optimal 1k minimum size requirement for the intersection, our work represents an significant enhancement to the 3k-4 conjecture and has far-reaching applications to the study of additive combinatorics. Furthermore, our technique likely holds significant potential for future research and development. Lastly, while the additive aspect of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture is the most well-known, our proof in fact addresses the more general version of the conjecture that applies to arbitrary finite groups, as proven by Ruzsa in 2001. Our approach in this instance relies heavily on Ruzsa's innovative solution to the problem. The development of social relationship graphs has far-reaching implications for various applications such as data interchange, data integration, and information sharing across multiple platforms. Nevertheless, the task of accurately mapping users to their respective groups and individuals to their respective connections in a graph is a persisting challenge, particularly in datasets lacking comprehensive label information. In this paper, we introduce a novel comprehensive network, denoted as ComNet, aimed at generating social relationship graphs where nodes are connected to each other through meaningful relationships. To this end, we employ a node embedding technique that leverages the structural attributes of a network to guide an unsupervised grouping process and improve connection accuracy. In contrast to existing methods, ComNet levers multiple network views to fine-tune node embeddings, thereby resulting in improved supervised graph creation. We evaluate ComNet's efficacy on five real-world datasets, where it consistently outperforms existing approaches in both grouping and connection accuracy. Notably, ComNet achieves a 87.38% grouping accuracy and 88.53% connection accuracy on the Yelp dataset. In a real-world scenario, ComNet demonstrates its ability to enhance various graph-based applications by 2.81%. In particular, an 8.21% relative improvement is observed in data interchange applications. Furthermore, ComNet is universally applicable to various graph-based applications as evidenced by its 2.81% overall enhancement in information sharing across multiple platforms. The source code of ComNet is publicly available at https://github.com/hbik/ComNet. In addition, the generated social relationship graphs based on ComNet are available at https://github.com/hbik/ComNet/tree/main/graphs. A compact muon collider is an innovative particle collider design that has the potential to serve as a preeminent Higgs factory and an advanced collider for studying subatomic particles. Due to the significant progress in accelerator and muon storage ring technology in recent years, constructing such a collider has become more feasible. Various research groups in the US have advanced conceptual designs for a muon collider, addressing challenges including cooling and storage, taking into account the difficulties of muon production, acceleration, and handling. A major issue hindering progress is the lack of a muon ionization cooling technology, which poses an obstacle for implementing a muon collider. Establishing a muon collider will require the development of a dedicated muon storage facility and may necessitate a new, purpose-built site. Prioritizing this project is essential to meet the growing demand for more powerful and versatile particle colliders in the future. 

In this talk, we will cover the following points:

* An update on the state-of-the-art in muon collider concepts will be provided.
* An overview of the challenges and obstacles in muon collider development will be presented.
* In particular, we will focus on the cooling and re-cooling technology requirements for muon colliders.
* An assessment of the feasibility of constructing a muon collider in the US context will be included.
* Finally, we will conclude by highlighting the broader implications of muon collider development for future particle physics research and technology development.
