Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity to a given input vertex. Previously, no PTAS existed for general-weighted CSPs, even on specific graph classes like interval graphs. Our research provides a PTAS for a broad class of CSPs that includes vertex or edge independent problems, such as Minimum Vertex Cover, as a special case. The key assumption is that the CSP has a guarentee that can be calculated efficiently within a factor of O(n) for an input graph with n vertices. Our technique develops a new framework that applies to graph classes with specific structural properties and offers insights into the nature of CSPs. Furthermore, this method sheds light on the previously complex Minimum Vertex Cover - Multiway Cut equivalence problem on general-weighted CSPs. By slightly modifying the approach, we obtain a PTAS for the Minimum Vertex Cover, Maximum Coloring, and Minimum Independent Domination problems on graph classes that are 2-vertex or edge partitionable. Our work presents a notable connection between the Minimum Vertex Cover and Maximum Coloring problems under this new partitionability criterion. Finally, our research reveals that the Minimum Vertex Cover - Multiway Cut equivalence problem can be solved efficiently on graph classes that are 2-vertex or edge partitionable. One notable example of such a class includes interval graphs. Until now, no PTAS existed for minimum-weight general-weighted CSPs on interval graphs, even though a PTAS existed for the maximum independent set problem. Our research provides an efficient solution that runs in O(n^ω vc) time, where vc represents the number of vertices in the vertex cover of the input graph. As another application of our new framework, we obtain a PTAS for the minimum-weight general-weighted CSP on circle graphs, along with the minimum vertex cover - multiway cut equivalence problem. The key challenge here lies in developing an efficient guarentee that can be calculated quickly. Our research provides an O(n)-factor guarentee that can be computed in O(n^2) time. Based on this guarentee, we obtain a PTAS that runs in O(n^ω vc) time. The maximum independent set problem, by contrast, could be solved more efficiently, with a PTAS running in O(n log n) time. Our work reveals an interesting connection between the minimum-weight general-weighted CSP and the minimum vertex cover or independent set problems, especially on graph classes that have specific structural properties.

Analyzing text aspects in various domains is crucial for understanding narratives, pinpointing system weaknesses, and uncovering hidden information. Current assessments of pre-trained language models are primarily confined to benchmarking their performance on fully annotated data sets, often neglecting their potential for making inferences with limited or no reference points within real-world scenarios. This study seeks to evaluate and establish new benchmarks that gauge a language model's ability to make informed inferences in both unmonitored and few-example situations. Our initial examination revolves around the analysis of clinical narratives, specifically focusing on uncovering system reviews and summarizing patient stories with limited context. The results reveal that certain pre-trained language models can excel in both unmonitored and few-example conditions, particularly when it comes to identifying system reviews, whereas for summarization, a few examples significantly boost the accuracy of generated outputs near ideal benchmarks. Interestingly, our findings also suggest that pre-trained language models can adapt to new tasks more effectively when their training is based on related datasets rather than generic web-scale data. Our created clinical-text dataset, along with the code and results, is made accessible for research purposes. This study aims to set a precedent for evaluating the boundaries of language models across diverse text contexts and few-example scenarios. This result further proves that RAM's sorting algorithm, previously believed to require linear time, can in fact run in linear time on the same model. Session-based recommendation is an active research area that has gained significant attention in recent years. The key challenge it poses is to make predictions for the next item in a user's browsing history without access to information outside the current session. One of the primary obstacles is the limited context available for model training. To address this issue, a new method called Self-Guided Graph Co-Training (SGGT) has been developed with the aim of enhancing recommendation quality by leveraging implicit feedback and graph embeddings within each user's interaction history. The core idea behind SGGT involves employing two distinct models that learn from two different aspects of the data: one fine-tunes existing models using ordered session information, while the other generates necessary guidance through an autoencoder-based representation learning process. By doing so, SGGT enables two models to learn from each other and improve their respective performance over time. Moreover, SGGT uses TRPO for joint training of the two models end-to-end, thereby maximizing the achievements of individual models. Experimental evaluations have shown that SGGT achieves superior performance on multiple benchmark datasets. Additionally, the proposed approach has been implemented with a transparent code availability for the sake of reproducibility. SGGT has outperformed state-of-the-art baselines in three benchmark datasets including TwoMovie, Yelp, Amazon. Moreover, SGGT has achieved a remarkable improvement of 5.08%, 8.33%, 6.42% in terms of MRR on these datasets respectively when compared with the best performing baseline. The highest achievable MRR of SGGT has been 0.6543, 0.7180, 0.6995 in terms of MRR on these datasets respectively. Also SGGT has achieved a remarkable improvement of 4.89%, 7.66%, 5.57% in terms of NDCG in Amazon, Yelp, TwoMovie respectively when compared with the best performing baseline. The highest achievable NDCG of SGGT has been 0.2074, 0.2511, 0.2243 in terms of NDCG in Amazon, Yelp, TwoMovie respectively. All experiments have been conducted on two NVIDIA Tesla V100 16 GB GPU. The implementation of SGGT has involved 348 lines of code. Also there are 214 nodes in the graph of Amazon, 176 nodes in Yelp, 247 nodes in TwoMovie used for the sake of evaluation. Theoretical investigations of topological properties in systems without hermiticity are particularly relevant, given the ease of creating unhermitian configurations in experiments. Our research focuses on a non-Hermitian point-gap topology in a one-dimensional model, consisting of an array of quantum dots interacting with a laser and each other. Initially, the laser-induced dissipation creates a spectral gap at the point where the system's equilibrium Hamiltonian becomes flat. However, our findings demonstrate that even a simple two-body interaction can close this gap due to asymmetric radiation absorption by different sites. The gap closure occurs at an intermediate strength of interaction per site, leaving the system's topological properties unchanged but introducing flatband points, which might be observable through experimental detections of flatband correlations and localization. The system's dynamics shows stable emergence of long-lived transient flatband states, which could be probed by analyzing real-time correlations. Our research utilizes the density matrix approach to solve the open quantum system's master equation and models the interactions via an L\"uders evolution following a projective reduction scheme. The chosen scheme is justified by analyzing the system's projective block-diagonal representation and finding that the non-hermitian part's Fano-Luders eigenvalue lies very close to one. The close value of this eigenvalue around one supports the validity of projecting the system's density matrix onto its upper block and applying the L\"uders evolution, which leads to a fully transparent interaction and the system's reduction to a hermitian model that can be solved analytically to find its real-time correlations. By extending this solution to a wider range of interactions, our research reveals that nearly flatband correlations could be observed in various interacting scenarios, such as the regime where the system's dissipation-induced gap closes at the point where the system's equilibrium Hamiltonian becomes flat. Furthermore, our simulations show that real-time correlations in the system increase at the point where the system's dissipation-induced gap closes, which could be probed through measurements of flatband correlations and localization. The proposed model offers a suitable theoretical framework for understanding and analyzing flatband correlations in non-Hermitian systems, which could provide valuable insights into the topological properties of such systems, especially their prolonged transient states which may be observed in future experiments. The system's topological properties, such as edge states and flatband states, can be probed through measurements of correlations and various spectral properties. A novel category of golf club set arc set designs, referred to as golf set arc sets, is presented. These arc sets are comprised of a pair of arc sets, each consisting of n-1 arcs with each arc defined by a distinct rational point on the projective line over a finite field F_q. A unique property of golf set arc sets is the existence of a symmetric matrix associated with each arc in the set, with all entries being integers from the set {-1,0,1}. The total sum of matrix entries for each arc is also defined as an important property. A second matrix associated with each arc in the set is referred to as the Fourier matrix, with entries being the Fourier coefficients of a specific function over F_q. Both matrices play a crucial role in the theory and application of golf set arc sets. Altered regions in ORGANIC materials are difficult to detect, especially with limited spectral information available in standard sensors, as they often have spectral properties similar to healthy areas. In contrast, the rapid development of hyperspectral imaging systems allows for the capture of multiple spectral bands, aiding in alteration detection. Nevertheless, using and integrating multiple spectral bands poses challenges, particularly in processing and interrelating spectral channels. Current deep convolutional autoencoders addressing this issue overlook the interactions between spectral channels. In this research, a novel deep convolutional autoencoder model is introduced that integrates feature integration and learning to identify alterations in altered regions, especially in organic materials, as it incorporates multi-spectral information. The proposed method outperforms conventional approaches in alteration recognition and accurately identifies altered regions using a weighted fusion technique. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of this model in identifying alterations, particularly in organic materials. The associated code for this model is available at https://github.com/JaberKhaled/FCAn. The model was tested using EDFA-based hyperspectral images captured over 16 spectral channels ranging from 450 nm to 900 nm. The dataset was captured from altered regions in organic materials at the University of Baghdad's campus. The model was evaluated using three metrics: synthetic discriminant function, decision boundary, and multi-feature angle, and achieved a notable improvement in recognition accuracy compared to conventional methods. The proposed model achieved a high success rate of 95.75% in detecting alterations, significantly higher than the 68.63% achieved by conventional deep convolutional autoencoders. The model's effectiveness can be attributed to its ability to process multi-spectral information and integrate features, thus outperforming conventional approaches. The proposed method has several potential applications, particularly in fields like medicine and astrophysics, where the detection of alterations in multi-spectral images may lead to significant breakthroughs. Quantum information may leverage silicon's inherent properties to achieve significant advancements in processing and storage capabilities, particularly with the incorporation of silicon's unique valley degeneracy and associated physics. This research demonstrates the ability to control valley interaction within a single crystal of silicon by introducing a pair of carbon-based molecules at the molecular scale. Furthermore, this study establishes that valley interaction results in spin transfer between these molecules, which is directly supported by both theoretical models and experimental evidence obtained through use of electron spin resonance. Valleous coupling in silicon has been shown to be an effective mechanism for transferring information between regions of storage and processing areas within integrated circuits. However, an ERMR challenge may arise from valley-related interference in operations performed on stored spins, which could be mitigated by the employment of carbon-based molecules as valley filters. Nevertheless, if such molecules are utilized as means of spin transfer, then our findings suggest that valley-related interference could be directly manipulated and effectively eliminated. This research has contributed to our understanding of spin-valley interactions within complex systems and has also opened up new avenues for the design of next-generation quantum integrated circuits. Finally, while our study specifically focuses on a system comprising two molecules, our proposed theoretical model suggests that valley interaction could potentially be applied to a wide range of other spin-based configurations within silicon. Indeed, an ESR challenge may arise from determining the optimal positioning of groups of atoms within silicon, which could be directly manipulated to enhance performance of quantum integrated circuits. This research has presented a theoretical model that identifies such positions and, through use of experimental evidence, has also confirmed that these positions could be effectively realized through the use of electron spin resonance. This study has therefore demonstrated that valley interaction could be effectively applied to the design and development of integrated circuits featuring multiple quantum bits. This research has also identified a novel application for carbon-based molecules in silicon, which could be employed as means of information transfer, as well as a means of filtering valley-related interference. Finally, while our study specifically focuses on a valley-based mechanism for spin transfer, our theoretical model suggests that a wide range of other mechanisms - such as electromagnetic interaction - may also be employed to transfer information between regions of storage and processing areas within integrated circuits. This research has therefore contributed to our understanding of the design and development of integrated circuits featuring multiple quantum bits, which could be directly manipulated through use of electron spin resonance. Lastly, while our theoretical model focuses on a system comprising two molecules, our study specifically examines the application of valley interaction in integrated circuits featuring only a single quantum bit. Optimization methods have become a critical component for training modern energy-efficient models.  Thanks to their versatility, they have been applied in various domains such as neuroscience, signal processing, and image processing.  Despite their success, typical simulations require manual code modifications and can take weeks or even months to set up.  There is an acute need for a framework that streamlines the development and prototyping of open-source optimization methods, addressing issues of code fragmentation and vulnerability to software bugs.  We introduce LibOPT, a comprehensive Python library that addresses this challenge by providing a unique, modular architecture for implementing optimization methods and efficiently evaluating their performance across a wide array of applications and evaluation metrics.  Through a detailed case study involving 10 established methods, we showcase LibOPT's capabilities, prototype new hybridized and customized approaches, and highlight their comparative benefits, demonstrating the potential for hybridizing optimization methods with domain-specific expertise and introducing tailored algorithms with improved performance.  We also release LibOPT as an open-source resource for the community, along with the code and demonstration video available at: https://github.com/corlllib/LibOPT and https://cstex.github.io/LibOPTDemo/.  Leveraging LibOPT, researchers can accelerate their investigations, prototyping new optimization methods and validating their performance in diverse scenarios.  In turn, this is expected to lead to a surge in innovative ideas, further advancing the development of soft optimization methods.  Conversely, an inadequate understanding of optimization methodology hinders progress in various fields, with researchers often adopting a "shoot-and-pray" approach that compromises the robustness and reliability of existing models.  By addressing this knowledge gap, LibOPT includes a wide range of high-level tools for developing optimization methods, complemented by a comprehensive tutorial and annotated examples, empowering users to explore the underlying methodology.  Through a series of workshops and seminars, we have effectively taught researchers to use LibOPT, even with no prior knowledge of optimization, and have inspired new ideas, paving the way for a brighter future in expert-driven, customization of optimization methods.  By comparing the performance of optimization methods on model-dependent and model-independent metrics, we have demonstrated the potential for hybridizing these techniques with domain-specific knowledge and introducing tailored algorithms with improved performance. We establish a novel category of smooth algebraic varieties known as uniformly
polynomial varieties, where all mapping functions from one variety to another
satisfy a specific polynomial equivalence within a predetermined error margin.
Furthermore, we introduce the transferability degree, an innovation in degree
theory encompassing non- polynomial functions, revealing that it is a singular
metric. The introduction of this new degree leads to an enhanced understanding of
pointwise convergence and generalizes the concept of uniform convergence in
function spaces. Moreover, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for
achieving polynomial transferability using only basic algebraic operations. 
Finally, we apply this new concept to the study of smooth function approximation
and show that a function can be accurately approximated within a specified error
margin using polynomial functions defined on a particular domain. The
introduction of this new degree of smoothness bridges the gap between the
approximation of smooth functions and those from the broader class of
differentiable functions. This research further demonstrates that the concept
of transferability is not exclusive to real-valued functions but can also be
applied to functions with more nuanced value sets, such as complex or
grassmannian-valued functions. The general approach to measuring transferability
can also be applied to the study of other homomorphisms between algebraic
varieties, such as rank-1 tensor transferability. This novel perspective on
transferability degree also enables a more comprehensive understanding of the
concept of homotopy degree. By redefining the homotopy degree as the
transferability degree of a 1-dimensional tensor, we derive a simplified
formula for calculating homotopy degree and demonstrate that it is a singular
metric. The introduction of this new degree of homotopy leads to a more
characteristic and efficient description of the concept. Furthermore, we show
that the sample degree, an innovation in degree theory introduced by J. M.
Wright and C. W. Wulfram, is equivalent to the transferability degree of a 2-dimensional tensor. This new understanding of sample degree reveals that it
is a singular metric. The replacement of pointwise degree with transferability
degree and sample degree leads to a more concise and characteristic description
of these concepts. Lastly, we apply the concepts of transferability degree and
sample degree to the study of mapping functions defined on algebraic varieties,
such as smooth manifolds, and demonstrate that these degree theories can be
applied to the study of any smooth variety

In the framework of non-commutative spacetime, the quantum nature of field operators is examined in terms of their product and the commutator within the context of distributions. It is demonstrated that any identity of the field, whether it adheres to Wightman or Owen identities, will inevitably result in singularities of distributions. These singularities have implications that suggest objects like particles or fields may exhibit dual behaviors, yet it remains to be determined whether this duality translates to multiple states of matter or a single entity in varying states. Furthermore, a proposed identification of the field with its gradient, although providing a potential source of charge, remains inconclusive as to the source of charge itself. Ultimately, the identities examined, whether Wightman or Owen, fail to definitively identify quantum entities in non-commutative spacetime based on distribution analysis. Meanwhile, the observed duality of charge sources poses an interesting question: can the field and its gradient be seen as manifestations of a singular entity that speaks to the dual nature of observables in quantum theory? This duality, we propose, is not a result of charge but rather a fundamental property of quantum objects where, much like Schrödinger's wave and particle duality, duality is inherent to quantum theory itself. In essence, we pose the question of whether identifying a quantum entity poses a insurmountable challenge to duality? Finally, considering the observed duality of charge sources, we suggest that a more appropriate distribution for examining entity identity might be derived from the product of two quantum field observables rather than their commutator. In this context, we raise the possibility that identifications like Wightman and Owen, obtained from the commutator, may be superseded by a more relevant identification of quantum entities, namely the Peierls map. Unlike the examined identities, this identification derives from the product of two quantum field observables and has been successfully demonstrated in non-commutative spacetime. Thus, we propose the Peierls map as a more relevant identification of quantum entities where the field's identity is not just a singular entity but a dual entity. In contrast to our analysis based on charge sources, this identification presents a breakthrough where the dual nature of quantum objects, whether entities or fields, can be effectively demonstrated and observed. Hence, we suggest that a more relevant identification of quantum entities might be derived not from the examined Wightman or Owen identities based on charge sources but rather from the Peierls map. We introduce an innovative technique, two-photon absorption boundary transient-current technique (TPTC), for mapping electrical properties of materials. Specifically, we apply TPTC to study charge conduction in scCVD diamond by measuring transient currents resulting from two-photon absorption at different intensities. Our approach utilizes a nanosecond laser source and enables us to create detailed 3D profiles of charge conduction. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of in situ charge conduction mapping during growth, opening up possibilities for real-time examination of charge conduction in diamond and other materials. Our technique has particular relevance to diamond, with potential applications including charge conduction detection in diamond substrates used in quantum computing and charge transport in biological and medical sensors involving diamond. Additionally, this method could be adapted to study a range of other materials and devices. A comprehensive examination of charge conduction in scCVD diamond under various conditions is also contemplated. A computational model will be developed to analyze and optimize charge conduction in diamond and other materials, and this method will be compared to established techniques such as photochemical etching and R2D2 scanning. TPTC has the potential to become a crucial tool for charge conduction detection and mapping, enabling in situ 3D charge conduction analysis during diamond growth and elsewhere. A start-up company will be established to commercialize this technique and its applications. A major project is also planned to demonstrate the use of TPTC in scanning and detecting diamond substrates for quantum computing and other biological and medical applications. A broader outreach program will be involved in educating the public and training users in the novel TPTC technique and its many applications. As a corresponding member of I2PS, I will oversee the scientific development and commercialization of TPTC and related technologies. Also, I will direct the associated research and innovation activities involving university students, postdoctoral researchers, and other research community members. A notable achievement will be the establishment of a major research and innovation hub at U of T focused on diamond and other materials, with a strong emphasis on charge conduction detection and mapping. Moreover, I will lead the development of key educational programs at U of T in charge conduction-related topics, with a goal of educating the next generation of researchers and engineers. This will include a new and innovative graduate program in quantum engineering with a special focus on quantum diamond. Also, I will direct the development of online courses and educational resources in charge conduction for the broader public and educational communities. A related book project is also contemplated,

Arabic language social media platforms are increasingly saturated with misogynistic content, promoting hate speech towards women. This hate speech has severe impacts on society, spreading anxiety and fear among women. To combat it, machine learning-based systems can help identify and denounce hate speech. In this work, a deep neural network architecture is presented for detecting misogynic content and categorizing it into relevant themes. The proposed system's efficacy is demonstrated through an evaluation dataset of 9300 tweets, offering substantial insight into Arabic text classification. The study provides an in-depth examination of various approaches to one-shot learning for limited-data classification tasks. The proposed method is compared with current state-of-the-art techniques, showing improved performance and enhanced barriers against evasion tactics in Arabic text classification. The developed framework potentiality enables researchers to deploy this system on real-world platforms, providing a usable interface for users. The implemented framework, including associated code and data, is made available for reproduction of results. The study contributes to the literature by offering novel approaches to one-shot learning and integrating two distinct tasks: hate speech detection and theme classification. The proposed method addresses partial criticism in the related work, particularly from Bouazizi et al., by enhancing the barriers against misuse of the model's output. The study's findings offer novel contributions to the literature on Arabic text classification. The developed system is potentially suitable for use by digital platform moderators in balancing the need to enforce rules and respect users' speech freedoms. The study explores potential applications of the system in real-world contexts, such as content moderation on social media platforms. The involved researchers, including myself (Aminah Anjum), Mohammad Alhasan, and Dr. Fazle Rabbi, have made our code, data, and model publicly available for reproduction of results. The study provides an in-depth examination of our approach and compares it with state-of-the-art techniques, showcasing the system's performance on various benchmarks and evaluating its efficacy against diverse types of misogynic content. The associated demo video and model data can be accessed via the indicated links. The study's associated website offers additional information on the study, including code, data, and model downloads, as well as a demo of the system in action. The proposed method addresses the mentioned challenge by offering an innovative solution to one-shot learning in Arabic text classification. We introduce an innovative controller type called resilient timed safety controller, which can adapt to unexpected changes in a system's behavior dynamics while ensuring safe operation. Building upon the concept of resilience from dynamic fault tree analysis, we develop a model-checking and policy-exploration approach to identify robust control strategies for complex cyber-physical systems. Our approach involves driving the system through a stochastic trajectory using optimal control actions, while simultaneously analyzing the evolution of its environment and checking for deviations from expected behavior. As environmental parameters become active, the controller's action model and reward structure are updated in real-time to maximize resilience in the face of unexpected influences. Through a practical case study from the power grid domain, we showcase the efficacy of our approach in identifying robust control strategies capable of adapting to rare and previously unconsidered system failure patterns while ensuring safe and resilient operation. Our research findings have profound implications for the adaptive management of cyber-physical systems, encompassing topics such as performance scope and the cost of resilience. The underlying toolchain of our approach, comprising the model checker and policy explorer, is designed for independence from any particular notation and can be accessed via http://resilient-control.github.io/RTSC-Toolchain.html. The source code of the toolchain, along with additional technical details, is available at https://github.com/Resilient-Control.github.io/RTSC-Toolchain. This paper introduces a novel, comprehensive framework that encompasses various caching and decentralized computation schemes. By utilizing a hypothetical "encoder box" equipped with multiple input and output slots, the framework enables the creation of schemes for specific tasks, such as encoded caching and computation, by mapping slots to relevant information and establishing corresponding relationships. A general method for determining the minimum required number of slots is also presented, allowing for the development of optimized schemes with the lowest possible slot counts. Furthermore, this universal framework is applied to design novel schemes for caching and computation, which are then compared with existing methods in terms of slot usage. Specifically, the framework is used to develop a caching scheme with the reduced requirement of $\lceil \log_2 (n+1) \r{c}{2}$ storage slots and a computation scheme with the reduced requirement of $n$ execution rounds, where n represents the number of distributed data pieces. By comparing these results with the best existing performance, the superior efficiency of the proposed schemes is demonstrated in terms of slot usage in caching schemes and round count in computation schemes. Certain known schemes like P2C and MCC, however, exhibit better performance than the introduced schemes in certain scenarios, particularly in terms of a larger valid support range for P2C. By combining this universal framework with the concept of code property, a method for further enhancing the performance of P2C is presented. The introduction of this framework allows for the development of unified methods for evaluating the performance of caching and computation schemes, which should facilitate the design and analysis of such schemes in the future. The proposed universal framework is supported by the accompanying MATLAB code, which is publicly accessible at the specified link. This code facilitates the calculation of slot count for different schemes and compares their performance under various parameters. The introduced framework is believed to be original and novel in the field of encoded caching and decentralized computation schemes. Our development of the PCF framework follows Scott's framework and is based on a type of functions known as types of families, which can be understood as a specific form of univalent types. By doing so, we are able to establish a precise logical interpretation of PCF, which is grounded in the weakened type of dependent type theory. Furthermore, we establish a corollary showing that weakened type of dependent type theory with a specific set of basic non-recursive types is capable of replicating the full computational power of PCF. Lastly, we define a notion of weakening for PCF and demonstrate that its semantics can be subjected to this weakening, which in turn corresponds to a specific form of currying. Ultimately, this entire development is set within the parameters of a weakened type of dependent type theory. Rather than incorporating recursion into the basic type system, our development makes use of a distinct recursion principle that operates at the level of types of families. This distinct recursion principle is itself grounded in a fundamental concept known as full coherence, which serves as a key component in the body of work on univalent mathematics. It is notable that the full coherence itself does not pose a threat to consistency, as it can be seen as an iterative definition. Moreover, our development makes use of a weakened version of universality, which can be seen as an iterative definition as well. These versions of full coherence and weakened universality are discussed at length in a separate paper. In what follows, we draw upon key insights from this body of work as we establish our development of the PCF framework within the parameters of a weakened type of dependent type theory. PCF with weakening draws upon key insights from another project, in which we applied the techniques of a weakened type of dependent type theory to the analysis of the Böhm-Berarducci translation. It achieves this by incorporating a distinct recursion principle, an altered notion of weakening, and an interpretation of the PCF type family that is grounded in a type of families. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weakened type of dependent type theory with recursion and the Böhm-Berarducci translation are compatible with one another. Finally, we show that the fundamental computational concepts of the weakened type of dependent type theory and the Böhm-Berarducci translation can be recovered from the weakened type of dependent type theory with recursion. This set of matrices forms a subgroup within the general linear group $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. A specific type of Eisenstein series, referred to as a generic Eisenstein series, can be defined using a generic $UT(n, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$-double coset representative. This generic Eisenstein series has poles at specific points, which we aim to eliminate through the application of an adjoint action based on Weyl elements. By examining the combinatorial structure of the matrix actions, we can analyze the effects of the adjoint actions on the generic Eisenstein series. Ultimately, this study seeks to understand how the adjoint actions modify the asymptotic properties of the generic Eisenstein series. This paper focuses on a key aspect: computing the local factors that combine to give the asymptotic cancellation of matrix action-affected generic Eisenstein series. A key challenge lies in determining the local factors of the adjoint actions based on the omega-Satake maps. This paper establishes a formula that computes the local factor of a specific action, which involves the character of a certain irreducible representation within the adjoint action. By utilizing character decompositions, we can calculate the local factor for any action. Notably, our analysis focuses on a specific action, which results in a factor consisting of a product of three-space Eisenstein series at a specific point. By applying the Satake map, which relates the eigenspheres of a three-space to the classes of certain Hermitian forms, we can recharacterize the asymptotic cancellation property using the form classes as our new parameters. This map allows for a complete characterization of the generic Eisenstein series after all poles have been eliminated. This research introduces a groundbreaking approach to designing secure control methods for mobile robotic limbs, leveraging control barrier functions and configuration-dependent dynamics. A novel decoupled control design is presented that effectively mitigates input constraints and maintains system state within predetermined boundaries, by dividing the controller into a traditional and configuration-adjusted component. Building upon this framework, we develop a dynamic output feedback controller, capable of ensuring system security with partial state information. To validate the efficacy of this innovation, we conduct simulation experiments involving a 2D and 3D robotic walking sequence, demonstrating that the proposed controller is able to prevent system state from entering restricted regions and walk along predetermined paths. Moreover, we explore the geometric interpretation of these results. In projective terms, a nondegenerate point for a polynomial system $X$ occurs when none of its partial derivatives vanish at that point. Our method uses signature transformations to define a lattice polytope, which represents the nondegenerate region of $X$, and calculates its volume as a signature-oriented complexity measure. Our algorithm offers two significant advantages over existing methods: it has a lower worst-case computational complexity and can handle larger systems than before. Moreover, it can be implemented more efficiently using available software libraries than previously possible. Using this method, we are able to reproduce known results for previously challenging polynomial systems and obtain new volume counts for previously intractable systems. Our study also explores the limitations of this method in determining the dimension of the nondegenerate component and identifies examples where the method provides an exact dimension, offering partial answers to previously open questions. Finally, we propose further research directions based on the insights gained from this study. Our methods are accompanied by accompanying code available at \href{ https://github.com/nus-equivolume/SignatureVol\_code}{github.com/nus-equivolume/SignatureVol_code}. The code specifically addresses the calculations described in Sections \ref{sec:extension}, \ref{sec:dimension}, and \ref{sec:futuredirections}. Complete elimination of line aliasing on vector maps through rendering is highly impractical due to the considerable computational resources required, especially when dealing with complex city map illustrations. This is primarily because the traditional anti-aliasing technique involves replicating each line segment and calculating its interpolation values in the output pixel zone. In this research, we introduce an efficient anti-aliasing technique for line mapping, reducing the computational burden by reusing calculated interpolation values along a line. Additionally, we modified this approach to accommodate mapping scales and integrated it with a line simplification method to strike a balance between rendering quality and processing speed. Specifically, we implemented an innovative spatial anti-aliasing technique for line mapping, based on a map's tile partitioning system, which takes into account the unique characteristics of cartographic illustrations and the limitations of human vision. This technique enables the efficient rendering of alias-free line connections on vector maps, achieving a 50% reduction in rendering time compared to the standard anti-aliasing technique. Furthermore, we analyzed the effects of line simplification on rendering quality and identified an optimal balance point, demonstrating that line simplification can preserve the quality of complex city map illustrations while reducing the rendering computational burden by up to 80%. A system prototype was developed and evaluated through on-street testing, confirming the feasibility and effectiveness of the presented anti-aliasing technique and line simplification strategy. Notably, this technique also addresses the distinct requirements of cartographic illustrations, marking an innovation over conventional anti-aliasing methods. The success of this research opens up the possibility of applying the presented techniques to a broader range of map-based applications. In particular, we identified an alternative solution to the long-standing (anti-aliased outline rendering is too computationally intensive) issue encountered in the field. Additionally, this research demonstrates the potential of combining anti-aliasing and line simplification, two previously unrelated techniques, to achieve a common goal. A line simplification strategy was developed to strike a balance between rendering quality and processing speed, thereby facilitating the efficient presentation of complex city map illustrations on minimal-resource devices. Lastly, a map's aesthetic quality was incorporated into the anti-aliasing technique, taking into account factors such as color and visual consistency to ensure that alias-free line connections are presented in a visually appealing and coherent manner. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have seen significant advancement in image recognition, however their application in climate classification is quite limited. This study introduces an original multi-class dataset consisting of 248 weather condition categories, derived from the integration of Wikipedia's climate and weather data for global cities. Additionally, this paper examines various evaluation methods used to assess CNN performance, specifically mean average precision (MAP) in addition to standard accuracy and F1 score. Our analysis also explores the impact of augmenting the dataset with synthetic images, notably by training a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), on the performance of CNNs. Finally, this study showcases the potential of CNNs in climate classification by achieving state-of-the-art results on the newly constructed dataset. The proposed dataset and associated code are accessible for review.

Our research focuses on the influence of social influences among climate change experts. An online survey was conducted with climate change researchers and professionals in the field of economics, who were asked to rate the effectiveness of various climate change mitigation measures. The results revealed that these experts tend to favor measures supported by a majority of other experts in the field. This phenomenon was most pronounced among economists, who showed a clear preference for measures backed by a larger number of experts. In contrast, scientists at different stages of their career and with varying levels of job security tended to favor measures that are popular among their peers, but did not display the same level of consistency in their preferences. The findings of this study highlight the importance of social influences among climate change experts and suggest that understanding these influences can contribute to the effective implementation of climate change policies. The expert network underlying the preferences of these professionals is dynamic and constantly evolving. The results of this study also highlight the distinct characteristics of different groups within the field of climate change and suggest that their respective values and priorities should be taken into account in climate change policy-making processes. Our research does not provide evidence to support the idea that experts tend to favor policies supported by a majority of other experts simply because of their popularity. Rather, their preferences are closely linked to their understanding of the expert network and the perceived authority of their peers. The usage of soft grippers in handling delicate objects is a compelling idea, but it requires complex control analysis due to the high nonlinearity involved, thereby needing a control method that simplifies this analysis. This study proposes using the Koopman operator theory to simplify the analysis of soft grippers, which are modeled using Finite Element Methods (FEM) and simulated with the L2-Solvers Method. By applying the KOM, it's possible to transform the complicated partial differential equations into a linear set of ordinary differential equations, making it easier to analyze the system's stability and perform feedback control design. Additionally, the study's results show that the control design and the use of virtual models can improve the efficiency of soft gripper control in real-world applications. This research presents a groundbreaking approach to digital twin-based control design for nonlinear soft grippers, offering a significant advantage over existing models. Moreover, this study's innovation in applying the KOM to digital twins has numerous applications across multiple domains. Recent breakthroughs in open-domain conversation models using large language models have demonstrated significant progress, but yet to be achieved is a comprehensive framework capable of managing various types of conversations. The majority of existing approaches concentrate on a single style of conversation, such as multiple choice, conversational question-answering, or text generation, employing similar methodologies in each case. In real-world scenarios, multiple forms of human interaction exist, like interviews, presentations, and meetings, which cannot be adequately addressed through current models. In response to this gap, we have developed a universal framework to handle diverse conversation roles, utilizing a combination of non-parmetric and structured approaches that are compatible with both few-shot and zero-shot techniques. The introduction of this framework to the community through open-source access may facilitate further advancements in this domain. In addition to presenting our approach, we also introduce a comprehensive dataset comprised of 386,298 human-like conversation turns across 48 distinct roles, referred to as the Role Defined Open-Domain Conversation Dataset (RDOC-D), collected through an automatic writing process that ensures high quality standards. Our approach consistently outperforms the best available methods in numerous evaluation metrics by a significant margin of 14.60% in terms of overall performance. In specific contexts, the difference in performance sometimes reaches as high as a 312.98% improvement. In contrast to other methods, our approach is also capable of adapting quickly to new conversation roles, achieving a remarkable 94.44% success rate in a zero-shot evaluation. A comprehensive comparison with other top models in this space, along with the proposed RDOC-D dataset and our code, have been made available for reproduction of results at: https://github.com/aleaf17/RDC-Few-Shot and https://github.com/aleaf17/RDC-Zero-Shot. A video explaining our approach is available at: https://youtu.be/6Oj4, and an interactive demo can be accessed at: https://rdoc-demo.herokuapp.com/. A key issue in artificial intelligence is the transfer of knowledge from one domain to another, particularly when it comes to the emergence of new concepts. Currently, most methods that facilitate knowledge transfer or enable the emergence of new concepts require extensive labeled data, are confined to specific domains, or model a single aspect of the target domain. To address these challenges, we've developed an innovative approach called the signaling game for broad, multi-faceted knowledge transfer. In this approach, a sender seeks to convey a hidden'semantic content' to a receiver through a binary channel, and a learner seeks to infer that content based on the sender's binary signals. Importantly, as the sender and learner interact, the semantic content and binary signals are co-learned. Through experiments on tasks such as intent recognition, data interpretation, and concept emergence, our approach has demonstrated superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets. Crucially, the emerging concepts developed by our approach are found to be semantically coherent and actionable. Additionally, the underlying knowledge transfer mechanism underlying our approach is seen as analogous to natural language semantic changes. To validate the emergent concepts and evaluate the knowledge transfer, we've also created a set of qualitative challenge tasks. Inspired by a recent hypothesis, our results from these tasks suggest that the emergent concepts, as the learner infers from the binary signals, may reflect the underlying knowledge that the sender is trying to convey. Furthermore, the knowledge transfer mechanism of our approach, as the sender and learner interact, is seen as akin to a bargaining process in economic terms. Based on this finding, we've also devised a set of quantitative metrics to evaluate the knowledge transfer and the emergent concepts. Through experiments on the benchmark datasets, our results using these metrics have shown that the knowledge transfer and the emergent concepts develop in a predictable and gradual pattern. To further validate the knowledge transfer and the emergent concepts, as well as the signaling game paradigm, we've also involved human subjects in a crowdsourcing study. Through this study, we've demonstrated that the knowledge transfer and the emergent concepts are not only predictable but also understandable to human learners. Ultimately, we've showcased a video that illustrates the knowledge transfer and the emergent concepts in real-time as the sender and learner interact. To facilitate reproducibility, we've also made available the source code, the benchmark datasets, the crowd-sourced data, and the video. A ordinary Hall effect occurs when two current carriers in an anisotropic material move at different speeds in response to an electric field normal to the direction of the charge carriers. This results in a non-zero transverse electric field for a given current direction. A thermal Hall effect can be observed when the charge carriers are instead excited by thermal means, at which point the transverse electric field is generated in response to a temperature gradient instead of a current. However, the thermal Hall effect is typically hindered in systems that are symmetric with respect to time due to zero Seebeck tensor. A new type of thermal Hall effect has been observed in a time-reversal symmetric system that may also be applicable to systems that previously displayed the anomalous thermal Hall effect. Furthermore, this study has discovered that the factors contributing to the thermal Hall effect are not equivalent to their electric counterparts, despite shared physical origins. Additionally, the relationships between energy, entropy, and heat, known as Einstein relations, were found to be violated in systems that exhibit the thermal Hall effect, at zero temperature. These relations typically describe the behavior of systems in contact with an heat bath. In place of the Einstein relations, a new set of relations was developed to accurately calculate the long-wavelength behavior of the local heat currents and their covariance. These relations can be used to calculate a zero-temperature local thermal conductivity from knowledge of the specific heat and velocity of the charge carriers. The covariance of the local heat currents was found to be proportional to the square of the velocity of the charge carriers and the gradient of the chemical potential with respect to the Frobenius number. In cases where the charge carriers' velocity is known and the gradient of the chemical potential with respect to the Frobenius number can be assumed to be constant, the local thermal conductivity can be expressed as the sum of a Drude contribution and a quantum contribution proportional to the Frobenius number. Ultimately, the thermal Hall effect was observed in a two-dimensional semiconductor system that was found to be time-reversal symmetric, at which point the Einstein relations were found to be breached in a zero-temperature system. The thermal Hall effect was observed to be a result of massless Dirac fermions that were found in the system, at higher temperatures, outside of the zero-temperature limit. During the training process of a neural network, its architecture's internal structure limits its capacity to form complex patterns. This limitation arises from the network's weight architecture, which imposes a series of constraints known as geometrical intricacy. To better understand this phenomenon, we introduced a set of regularizers that quantify the complexity of neural networks' weight graphs. By doing so, we demonstrated that these regularizers' constraints are reflected in the numerous simplifying invariants of neural network parameters and demonstrated that simpler patterns can sometimes be learned by neural networks due to these inherent limitations of their weight structures. This phenomenon has implications for neural network design and our understanding of their ability to represent complex patterns. Furthermore, we developed an algorithm to discover the most efficient and less complex representations of neural networks' weight structures. This method bears similarities to group action and orbit equivalence in dynamical systems and graph embedding algorithms. As a result, we obtained neural networks with reduced representation complexity and demonstrated their potential to surpass simple models in tasks requiring expressiveness and interpretability. The implementation details of our study, including the code, are available online at https://github.com/jbmanel/NeuralNetworkSimplifiers. A new approach for determining the four Wilson coefficients in the $b\to s$ interaction directly from experimental $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay data is proposed. This method leverages two observables derived from these decays, namely $R_K$ and $P_2$, to estimate Wilson coefficients. Unlike standard analyses based on maximum likelihood fits, this approach enables immediate assessment of uncertainties associated with Wilson coefficients using correlations within the same decay events without the need for fitting. This method's performance is demonstrated with Wilson coefficients from SM predictions and experimental data from LHCb. One notable outcome is the immediate identification of tensions within the same decay events involving new physics signals and control channels. This new approach can be applied to other $b\to s$ interactions and is particularly suitable for analyses involving $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays with ample event samples. On the other hand, it might not be the best choice for analyses involving events with low event counts such as $B_s\to K^+\mu^+\mu^-$ decays due to the high background levels in these cases. It is also worth noting that this new approach, while efficient, is not replacement for standard analyses but rather a tool that provides additional insights during data taking phases when statistics are limited but potentially indicative of new physics signals. Once sufficient statistics are attained, this new approach can be used to validate and confirm these new physics signals in various modes. It is further emphasized that this new approach can be adapted to work with new physics scenarios beyond the SM with next-to-leading order QCD contributions. On a related note, this new approach, in conjunction with tests involving other $b\to s$ interactions, can be utilized to determine the effective Wilson coefficients in dark matter models with new physics up to scales of $10^5$ GeV. The field of automated music composition is a rapidly evolving area, focusing on creating musical pieces partially or in entirety with the help of algorithms. One key aspect of this field is composition evaluation, which involves analyzing created music to determine its quality. Recent advancements in neural networks have led to the development of powerful new methods for music composition evaluation. However, insufficient data has become a significant challenge for this field, and methods to enhance and expand the available data are crucial. This work explores data enhancement techniques to expand a current dataset of human-rated quality assessments of generated musical themes. By applying techniques such as pitch-time stretching and pitch shifting to existing examples, the dataset is increased nearly fivefold. Additionally, the effectiveness of this approach is compared to that of a Transformer-based neural composition model in evaluating the quality of musical themes. Both methods demonstrate a notable improvement in the score compared to a baseline model in repeated experiments. It is well known that solving structured linear systems under varying right-hand sides presents an important problem in computational linear algebra, offering a challenge for algebraic approaches and potentially leading to significant speedups over generic solvers. Despite this, there has been limited research into systematically evaluating the toughness of algorithms in handling various systems, which is the focus of this study. We introduce a framework to measure toughness, allowing for comparisons of different solvers on a wide range of random linear systems with controlled properties. Using this framework, we test solvers for Toeplitz and circulant matrices, evaluating their performance and identifying the benchmarks where solvers may degrade or improve significantly. Our goal is to provide a standardized test suite to drive algorithmic innovation in solving structured linear systems. To this end, we also propose a new solver, WPT, which is based on the discrete Fourier matrix and is particularly effective in solving large-scale systems with small numbers of non-zero entries. Our objective is to facilitate healthy algorithmic and benchmark competition in this area. The code for the solver and the generated test suites are publicly available at https://github.com/yangchao112/Space-Toughness. Our numerical experiments show that WPT consistently outperforms other leading solvers in solving large-scale systems, and we have identified specific benchmarks where MGS outperforms WPT or FAS. Conversely, WPT remains the top performer in solving systems with prominent high-frequency components. Our study also reveals that WPT can provide notable speedups over WFLMAT and FFT-based solvers in certain scenarios, and we have found a general strategy to modify WPT and make it superior to WFLMAT. Furthermore, our algorithm remains effective even on modern GPU architectures, and we have found that WPT consistently outperforms WFLMAT or FFT-based solvers by 2-3 times in solving 10Kx10K systems on NVIDIA V100, AMD W7200, and Google TPUs. Our study also provides theoretical insights into when WPT can be superior to WFLMAT or FFT-based solvers. Specifically, we proved that WPT is more efficient than WFLMAT or FFT-based solvers when solving systems with prominent high-frequency components, and we provided a simple formula to estimate when WPT can be superior to WFLMAT or FFT-based solers. Furthermore, we revealed that WPT can provide notable speedups over WFLMAT or FFT-based solers in solving systems with multi-level non-zero patterns. Our study also provided a general strategy to modify WPT

In robust graph decentralized learning, the local data distributions on each node can vary significantly, and sudden changes in the network topology may occur, further exacerbating disparities between nodes. To tackle these challenges, we're introducing a groundbreaking and robust decentralized learning method called Distributionally Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD). DR-DSGD goes beyond current methods in several key ways: It doesn't rely on specific distributional assumptions beyond knowledge of mean shifts among neighbors; It doesn't require a fully connected network, and it's capable of adapting to topological changes. By leveraging boldness and caution in its update rules, DR-DSGD simultaneously minimizes local cost and mitigates distributional risk. We've established that DR-DSGD achieves optimal convergence. Even in the worst-case scenario, DR-DSGD's communication efficiency surpasses current methods, such as Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD), by a factor of $3.52$, and it also outperforms recent robust methods, such as SCHEDULE and GRAPE, by a factor of $10.5$ to $20.8. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets have demonstrated DR-DSGD's robustness and superior communication efficiency compared to current methods. To facilitate its adoption, we've also released DR-DSGD's code. DR-DSGD's integration of boldness and caution in node updates has allowed it to robustly adapt to changes in multi-node graphs while minimizing communication efficiency. This research focuses on the issue of efficient saturation in constrained nonlinear systems with parameters. An approach is developed to create a feedback policy that equilibrates competing costs: one for excessive output magnitude and another for deviation from optimal parameter settings. An optimal feedback controller is devised for a system with known output constraints using a piecewise linear and piecewise smooth strategy. Furthermore, this study investigates the problem of parameter deviation, formulating it as a nonlinear optimization issue with an efficient saturation component. An equilibrium between excessive output and parameter discrepancy costs is achieved through the use of a Lagrange multiplier in the optimal control theory. This result is further analyzed in the context of a example system from a domain called Chaplygin sailboats. Additionally, this research considers the scenario of time-varying parameters and proposes an algorithm to address this issue. This study makes available both MATLAB tools for reproducing the figures and a demonstration video. For the half-Cauchy distribution, establishing a confidence interval and interval square for the parameter $\sigma$ is particularly challenging due to its undefined mean and variance. This work overcomes this difficulty by employing an innovative approach that directly relates a parameter interval to a region on the parameter space, thereby circumventing the need for a distribution mean. Subsequently, this method is utilized to derive both symmetric and asymmetric confidence intervals for $\sigma$. Moreover, this article addresses the parameter estimation of the Cauchy distribution in two scenarios: unbiased and biased estimation. Notably, the estimators' distributions deviate from the standard cauchy distribution, and their variances can be calculated analytically. Ultimately, this article examines the estimation of the parameter $\sigma$ using both L2 and L1 distance metrics and demonstrates that the estimators exhibit consistent and asymptotic normal behavior. Furthermore, this article is the first to introduce a measure of squared confidence for the parameter $\sigma$ that is based on the concept of interval squares, enabling comparisons between different estimators and confidence intervals on a parameter-dependent basis. The proposed ideas are substantiated through simulations and real-world data analysis. This article presents software implementation specific to R. A new statistical method is proposed for estimating the sample size required in clinical trials where treatment effects are evaluated across multiple subpopulations defined by different covariates. This approach utilizes Bayesian statistics to combine data from individual subgroups and aims to increase efficiency by allowing for the transfer of information between subgroups and the simultaneous analysis of multiple endpoints across various subgroups. The method in question estimates the sample size needed in a new trial by calculating the required sample size for each subgroup individually using Bayesian principles, taking into account the achievable power and type I error rates, and then summarizing the results through measures such as the mean, median, and interquartile range to obtain a final sample size estimate and the associated range. The performance of this approach is evaluated in scenarios involving basket trials with multiple subgroups and varying numbers of binary endpoints and covariates, and it shows improved power and reduced required sample sizes compared to traditional methods for estimating sample sizes in clinical trials. Furthermore, the approach exhibits flexibility in handling various clinical trial scenarios and can be easily implemented in statistical software for practical use in research. Two real-world examples are provided to demonstrate the method's applications in practical scenarios, and simulations are conducted to evaluate its performance. The approach in question complies with current guidelines for estimating sample sizes in clinical trials and holds promise for being a useful tool in statistical research and practice. We introduce a novel deep learning network called Partial Registration network, or PRNet for partial-to-partial object alignment, taking into account the inherent partiality inherent in many objects. Unlike existing methods that focus on whole-to-whole object alignment, we leverage partiality constraints by employing a self-guided loss function. Initially, we normalize the input images to fix their scales and remove excessive ambiguity. Next, we define two registration modules that perform coarse and fine alignment, driving the network to converge towards a stable solution. A new strategy, called sturdy trajectory optimization, has been developed to efficiently analyze and interpret high-frequency data from advanced sensors, such as spectrometers and interferometers. We demonstrate the power of this strategy by applying it to the analysis of pump-probe spectra, a technique that measures the temporary impact of lasers on molecules to determine their structural dynamics. We describe a sturdy approach to optimizing spectral trajectories that identifies reliable solutions resistant to noise and other data imperfections. Additionally, we propose a method for implementing these optimizations using machine learning techniques. Our approach is evaluated on various data sets, including synthetic data based on quantum mechanical simulations of the response of molecules to laser pulses and actual experimental data from X-ray scattering experiments on molecules. We find that this sturdy strategy is highly effective in accurately determining the dynamics of molecules from both types of data. One particular algorithm from the sturdy family, called the stochastic trajectory optimization algorithm, is found to be particularly efficient and capable of interpreting data at a rate of millions of data points per second. Our findings indicate that this low-latency algorithm is well-suited to the analysis of data from broadband spectrometers, such as those used in future X-ray free-electron lasers, and has the potential to greatly expand our understanding of molecular dynamics. In addition to its potential applications in physics, we believe that our strategy has the capacity to significantly and positively impact a wide range of fields, including astrophysics, geophysics, and bio-science, where there is a growing need for efficient analysis methods. Specifically, the strategy could be used to better understand the behavior of galaxies based on data from radio telescopes and the movement of planets in the solar system determined from data from radar sensors. Furthermore, the strategy has the capacity to significantly contribute to the understanding of protein dynamics, the behavior of electrons in materials, and the detection of counterfeit currency based on data from various types of spectrometers. In summary, we believe that our approach, with its focus on robust and real-time analysis of data, has the potential to greatly expand our understanding of the world around us. This new understanding offers a more precise generalization of earlier research by many authors, and it selects a specific set of Gelfand-Shilov space categories where Toeplitz operators are known to be bounded, namely when the spaces have total smoothness greater than one. Moreover, our research demonstrates that Toeplitz operators with symbols that have linear polynomial forms are not bounded within Gelfand-Shilov spaces with total smoothness less than one. A cutting-edge approach called Differentiable Rendering utilizes a disease model learned from synthetic images to analyze real-world images, generating a target-specific output. However, current models face several limitations, such as the need for labeled data, a limited understanding of domain-specific factors, and poor preservation of data privacy. Our research addresses these constraints by introducing the Cycle Division GAN, which learns to divide unlabeled real images into instances to learn a disease model from unlabelled real images. Our approach consists of three components: (i) a self-attention mechanism that proposes similar pixels as a potential instance, (ii) a GAN that evaluates and filters proposed instances, and (iii) a cycle consistency loss that ensures discovered instances are consistent across image spaces. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method performs better than other state-of-the-art approaches, and we also analyze its runtime and model complexity. Our model is compatible with CRAN, an advanced technology for 3D data modelling. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. This research is novel in three ways: it's the first to discover instances from unlabeled real images, the first to apply differentiable rendering to 2D and 3D image spaces, and the first to perform instance division using a GAN. theory, and predicate logic with graded membership - that can reconstruct

antinomies known to arise from dealing with infinite quantities, particularly
the paradox of Zarathustra's ladder and the paradox of Lambs. Ultimately, we
will examine the results of handling these paradoxes within each framework.

This research paper explores the problem of accurately solving a polynomial linear system, particularly with coefficients that contain random errors. We apply techniques from probability theory and combinatorics to provide new bounds on the minimum number of points required to precisely locate a non-trivial solution's zeros. Additionally, we introduce a novel strategy to terminate the resolution process as soon as it becomes clear that a solution exists. This innovative approach significantly reduces the number of evaluations compared to traditional methods, offering improved efficiency and a thorough evaluation of its performance through extensive experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a complete interpolation system that can perfectly match any polynomial, highlighting its potential as a tool for robust polynomial interpolation and verification. This work also outlines future research directions and provides a comprehensive reference on solving polynomial linear systems with errors. We have also made the code associated with this paper available on GitHub under the MIT License, allowing for reproducibility and future distribution. To develop accurate predictions, we examined on-sky data from three observatories across different climates - the Atacama in Chile, the Mauna Kea in Hawaii, and the La Palma in the Canary Islands - to classify atmospheric models. Our models span from basic calculations for dust and water vapour to more complex representations, including a model that accounts for the variation in water vapour with altitude and another integrating the effects of dust and water vapour spectra. Our results reveal that the success of our atmospheric models in replicating on-sky measurements is influenced by several factors, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, and water vapour pressure. Our analysis also shows that the Mauna Kea and La Palma sites consistently exhibit higher agreement with our most advanced model than the Atacama site, likely due to variations in atmospheric conditions not captured by our measurements. The evaluation and enhancement of the classification skills in top-notch teachers for basic language comprehension tasks have shown notable improvements in recent years. Instead of individualized evaluation, grouping multiple instructors under the same training data and assessing their collective performance has become a more prevalent approach, known as multi-instructor labeled distillation. This method considers a cohort of teachers as a single distillation model, leveraging the existing knowledge and reducing the need for individualized supervision. However, existing multi-instructor labeled distillation techniques have shortcomings in self-supervised settings, particularly in the absence of labeled data, and often rely on augmented text to educate their teachers, which can be costly and time-consuming to prepare. To address these limitations, we introduce a new paradigm called PILE, based on the pair-wise iterative logging coalition framework, aimed at enhancing the skills of a cohort of teachers in the low-data, self-supervised regime. PILE utilizes a simple yet effective technique to exchange knowledge within the group of teachers, and we prove its superiority over existing approaches through comprehensive evaluations on tasks such as 20Semes and Multi-NaturalSettings. Our innovative approach not only outperforms traditional training methods but also surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art multi-instructor labeled distillation techniques, achieving a remarkable gain of 3.8 and 2.8 points in relative accuracy on SQuAD and NQS metrics, respectively. The source code for PILE is available at https://github.com/aleksie/pile.

A recent study has been conducted on three-dimensional chaotic scattering, particularly focusing on Wada basins that share borders with two distinct escape channels. Initially, it was found that increasing a parameter that controls escape rates in these systems enhances the area of Wada basins. Conversely, when this parameter reaches a critical value, the area of Wada basins begins to shrink, exhibiting non-scale, feeble dissipation effects. Furthermore, it was observed that Wada basins can still survive and even thrive in this scenario, providing a potential explanation for the longevity of Wada basins in nature. This research also opens doors for future investigations into the behaviors of Wada basins in various complex systems. Additionally, the study demonstrates that Wada basins can serve as indicators of transitions between different dynamics, thereby potentially utilizing them as controllers in applications such as search algorithms. The implications of these findings are substantial and warrant further exploration. The findings of this study contradict previous theories suggesting the complete disappearance of Wada basins in three-dimensional chaotic systems at a critical value of parameter 'q'. A key aspect of regularity theory in optimization lies in understanding how diverse solution sets can be. This idea is exemplified in multi-solution optimization, where multiple optima exist due to symmetries in the problem, leading to a population distribution in solution space. This distribution's diversity is influenced by several factors, including the degree of symmetry, solution set topology, and how populations are sampled. To study this effect, a methodological approach is taken, involving a simple multi-solution optimization problem in a real-valued space with known solution set topology. Variability in solution space is quantitatively analyzed for several different fitness functions. As a second step, a comprehensive search algorithm is developed to gather comprehensive data on solution space. Results from extensive computational searches are collected and examined. Finally, connections between solution space diversity and multi-solution optimizer design are explored, with suggestions for future research.
