In many situations, especially in housing, decision-making involves individuals or groups with both shared and individual interests who must cooperate to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome. A fundamental concept known as the housemates dilemma has been developed to study the interactions and outcomes of collaborative decisions within a group of self-interested and additively distinct agents, such as students living together in a dormitory. This paper focuses on a 3D version of the housemates dilemma, where a team of 3-6 students makes decisions within a small, enclosed environment represented by a cube, with each player having unique preferences for various properties and their combinations. Our findings reveal the precise requirements for the occurrence of the Pareto-drop and Nash-equilibrium-drop phenomena in this 3D setting, along with the relationship between these effects and the dimensionality of the environment. A comprehensive set of examples demonstrating the 1-dimensional constraint of the housemates dilemma in a simple 3D setting has also been established. Additionally, this paper explores the connection between the mathematical concepts of stable and Nash-equilibrium-indifferent outcomes. A key contribution of this research is the introduction of a new concept - outcome-priority. We have shown that outcome-priority is both necessary and sufficient for the occurrence of the housemates dilemma in a particular situation, essentially defining the 2-dimensional housemates dilemma. A comprehensive strategy for determining the occurrence of outcome-priority in any situation has also been established. In cases where outcome-priority is absent, we have developed a method to determine if a corresponding Nash-equilibrium-indifferent situation exists. A related inquiry in this research concerns the occurrence of the housemates dilemma when only considering marginal changes to individual preferences. A key contribution of this aspect is the introduction of a new concept - marginal-stable housemates dilemma. We have shown that the probability of the housemates dilemma and marginal-stable housemates dilemma occurring does not depend on the dimensionality of the environment and is therefore uniform for any number of dimensions greater than or equal to 3. Furthermore, we have found that while the probability of the housemates dilemma occurring is also uniform in environments with any number of dimensions greater than or equal to 4, this is not the case when considering only those situations in which all players have distinct preferences. In such cases, we have determined that the probability of the housemates dilemma occurring decreases as the number of dimensions increases and is therefore greater in 3D environments than in 4D, 5D, or 6D environments. We establish the definition of the Gromov-Hausdorff category of a metric space, 
leveraging on the concept of GH-decompositions and considering its category as a key property.
Then, by employing tree representations, we define the notion of GH-morphisms for certain structured spaces, 
which enables us to identify the central elements of these spaces and prove they form the basis of GH-decompositions.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that the set of central elements in a metric space possesses a natural partition, 
exposing its vast structural nature.
Lastly, two metric spaces are found to have a GH-decomposition with minimal category when their Hausdorff dimensions are both one. 
In other words, the category of a metric space does not necessarily imply its Hausdorff dimension. 
This research thus introduces a new concept and a new set of tools for metric space analysis, 
which is theoretically foundational and practically applicable. 
Given its novelty, this work is primarily intended for experts in the field. 
On the other hand, young scholars and those new to this subject may benefit from reading the introductory section and the appendix, 
which are designed to introduce the required theoretical underpinnings and provide comprehensive explanations. 
Ultimately, this paper aims to contribute to the extensive research on GH-decompositions and its various applications. 
As such, it is conjectured that the central elements of a metric space exhibit self-similar properties, 
which remains to be studied in the future. 
This research may also be extended by imposing additional requirements on GH-morphisms, 
such as preserving maps with specific properties, which is another area for potential future exploration. 
Lastly, this work is particularly dedicated to Liang-Neng Chang, who inspired this research, 
as well as Qinggang Chen, who provided valuable feedback and guidance, 
and especially to Ming-Fu Hu, who selflessly guided and supported my academic journey. 
Without their selfless support, this research would not have come to fruition. 
In the end, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to them all.

A fundamental issue in machine learning is the challenge of striking a balance between optimizing model performance and maintaining its ability to generalize. This problem is exacerbated by the presence of overfitting, where a model excels at predicting a specific training dataset but struggles with real-world data. In this research, we introduce Wealthy, a property development method that seeks to mitigate overfitting by utilizing diverse data attributes. Wealthy utilizes an inclusive approach to define new characteristics that 1) minimize reliance on noisy annotations from the training set and 2) maximize coverage of existing classes and data distributions. By virtue of these capabilities, Wealthy enables optimized models with enhanced generalization capabilities. As evidence, our method outperforms or rivals top-performing entities in tasks such as data compression, pseudo-labeling, and semi-supervised learning, while also introducing a versatile tool for feature engineering. This research is accompanied by a range of open-source code and empirical evaluations. Additionally, we have introduced the Anion benchmark, a resource for researchers seeking to address the optimization-generalization conundrum in machine learning. The Anion benchmark encompasses a diverse collection of 1) optimized-data challenges and 2) generalization-forced tasks, spanning multiple domains, to support the development of innovative solutions. This resource is poised to support the advancement of future research in machine learning. You can access the Anion benchmark at https://anion-benchmark.com/ and the source code for Wealthy at https://github.com/anion-benchmark/wealthy. You can learn more about the method in a companion paper at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48551/2206.14264. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the slow multiplication rate. To overcome this, researchers have proposed the small collection-electrode technology demonstrator (CLICTD), which incorporates active quenching and signal amplification, in combination with a highly sensitive single-photon detection system. This concept has been demonstrated in CMOS technology developed in 2015-2016. In this study, CLICTD's performance has been evaluated using different sensor thicknesses and substrates, tailored to be compatible with the CLIC detector research. Experimental data and simulation results are presented to investigate the sensor's time-use efficiency, active region length, hit output, and signal-to-noise ratio. Several major ground-based projects such as the Extremely Large Telescope, the Giant Magellan Telescope, and the James Webb Space Telescope plan to utilize advanced ATR and cryogenic detectors that operate in the near to mid-infrared spectrum to optimize performance. Despite this, their capacity to handle the anticipated mid-infrared speckers generated by atmospheric turbulence remains uncertain. A new approach called RASCS has been developed to enhance signal quality by extracting a reference from the speckles themselves. Recent RASCS simulations have demonstrated its potential to enhance performance of future instruments by increasing sensitivity, reducing flux loss, and allowing for broader bandwidths. This reference-based method appears to be effective even under conditions of high speckle velocity and severe atmospheric turbulence. We have now successfully implemented RASCS on a Santa Cruz type testbed that features a 64-pixel photodetector and operates within the 1.4 to 4.7 micron wavelength range, in addition to featuring a 4.5 meter diameter telescope. The testbed was used in experiments where it was subjected to various artificial speckles with velocities of up to 100 meters per second and a 4 to 200 meters dimension for the test signals. The results of these experiments have demonstrated the capability of RASCS to reduce speckle related noise by up to 80% and allow for as much as 4 times larger signal to noise ratios. The code used for these experiments has also been found to be scalable and capable of handling a range of up to 4 to 8 dimensional atmospheric parameters. This has implications for its potential use in future instrument designs. Data from these experiments has also been found to be compatible with the open source ZEMRAC code for phasing. This has implications for potential use of RASCS on future projects such as JWST, MIRADII-E, ELT, and GMT. This study presents a modified version of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, known as the CXIR model, to address the "deflation risk" issue in financial markets. The CXIR model ensures the likelihood of negative interest rates is zero, and it also maintains the conditions of the original mean-reverting process and the long-term mean being greater than zero. The main goal of this model is to reduce the potential for deflation and increase the likelihood of inflation. A key characteristic of this model is the addition of a linear "deterministic-shift" parameter that helps to prevent the occurrence of negative rates. The parameters of this model are estimated using two distinct estimation techniques: an iterative maximum likelihood method and a simulation-based approach. The results of these estimations indicate that the CXIR model offers a superior fit to real data compared to the original CIR model. Furthermore, empirical analysis suggests that the addition of the deterministic-shift parameter to the model enhances its ability to predict future movements in real interest rates. In addition, a simulation study confirms that the CXIR model remains stable and effective even at low sample lengths and extreme economic scenarios. The potential applications and advantages of using the CXIR model are discussed in relation to the use of long-term variable targets in monetary policy. A code for the model is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/abdelhakim-bouinu/CXIR_model. Meta-analyses including individual patient data are often encumbered with outcome-dependent dropout rates, rendering typical winBUGS Bayesian estimators unreliable due to up weighting dropout observations. In contrast, our new "stable" estimators - "cluster-stable" and "double-imputation stable" - guarantee reliable results regardless of dropout rates. Our approach builds upon existing methods, employing Bayesian extra-sensitivity and double imputation techniques to eliminate up weighting, utilizing cluster-level parameters and replicate data for the latter respectively. Through simulation, our proposed estimators outperformed traditional winBUGS estimators, with performance improving with increasing dropout rates and study numbers. Our approach also facilitates efficient computation via parallel processing and is both CPU and GPU compatible, with further speed enhancements achievable via Monte Carlo approximation and our companion R package's multi-threaded integration of compiled C++ functions. Ultimately, our "cluster-stable" estimator emerges as the preferred choice. In accordance with the principles of transparent research, our source code, R package and data are freely available at https://github.com/jbenny/constant-stable-MAMA. Our new stable estimators ensure reliable reverse trial meta-analyses free from up weighting biases, making individual patient data MAMA more reliable and practical. In contrast to frequentist approaches, our Bayesian solution provides a comprehensive one-size-fits-all solution applicable to various contexts, with our approach being compatible with widely used software and platforms. In particular, this method is poised to enhance the understanding and prediction of particle collisions in astrophysical events such as neutron star mergers. The findings of this study have also shed light on the importance of accurately modeling collision durations in turbulent flows. Moreover, the new algorithm significantly contributes to the advancement of particle simulation methods in general, thereby facilitating breakthroughs in various fields such as astrophysics and turbulent flows. Distorted galaxy morphologies, particularly 'u' type warps, are more prevalent in group and cluster settings. Our analysis revealed a marked association between jellyfish and warped galaxies (71% of distorted galaxies displayed jellyfish characteristics), with more pronounced 'j' shaped distortions among jellyfish galaxies. Furthermore, we found that 90% of distorted galaxies in groups were associated with clusters. These findings suggest that a common mechanism, possibly ram-pressure straining by a cluster-scale perspective, is responsible for both jellyfish and warped galaxy shapes. This could potentially be achieved through a collaborative effort between researchers and institutions. Additionally, we outlined key areas of research and the necessary steps to address these questions and refine our understanding of distorted galaxy phenomena in the future. This could involve incorporating new data, observing new phenomena, and refining our theoretical models of galaxy interaction and evolution. Specifically, we proposed the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to classify and study galaxy shapes, as well as the development of new gravitational N-body simulations to model galaxy interaction and the application of gravitational potencial to study distorted galaxy assembly.

A widely used method for estimating the average composition of a blend involves using measurements from a random sample of units, typically analyzers or tanks, whose compositions are considered independent and identically distributed realizations of a statistical population. This population is assumed to be normally distributed with known variance, allowing for the calculation of an unbiased maximum likelihood estimator of the average composition. When population parameters are unknown but variances are known, an asymptotically unbiased maximum likelihood estimator can be employed. This is particularly relevant in cases of limited sampling resources and known variances, such as when calculating the average yield of a batch process using batch variance or testing the purity of a drug using known variance of impurity measurements. It is further demonstrated that both estimators maintain desired properties, including consistency, asymptotic normality, and the ability to efficiently estimate variances. These results are illustrated through simulations of simulated and real-world data, including a case where a batch yield is estimated using process variances. A associated R function is provided for reproducing the results presented in the study. In the AS 209 protoplanetary disk, our previous MAPS observations detected a massive gas void at 88 au with a high CO J=2-1 column density, and this void surrounds two massive planet candidates. By analyzing the CO emission, we subtract the contributions of a power-law and a tenuous ring at 184 au. We observe that the CO emission inside the void is lower than expected by a factor of 5 to 6, and this factor does not change with the viewing angle. We investigate two theories. The first suggests that the void is formed by a planet that causes a gas gap, and the second implies that the void is created by a planet that causes chemical alteration. Our analysis shows that the void's shape and the CO emission ratio outside the gap are inconsistent with the first theory. Conversely, the second theory is consistent with the observed CO emission. Additionally, the gas void in AS 209 shows similarities to that in the HL Tau disk but differs from that in the TW Hydrae A disk. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the AS 209 massive void is likely the result of a planet-driven chemical alteration. Further observation of this target in the sub-millimeter and near-infrared spectral ranges is needed to distinguish between these theories. Achieving convergence with large datasets in Federated Learning is complicated due to two issues. Firstly, federated averaging is slow because local optimizers have varying convergence rates. Secondly, unconstrained gradients cause instability during aggregation. This paper tackles these challenges by introducing the Buffered Synchronous Aggregation (BSA) technique. BSA resolves the first issue by using a unified gradient at each round, derived from the last unconstrained vector of each worker's optimizer's trajectory. It also addresses the second issue by taking the average of these unified gradients. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that BSA surpasses existing Federated Learning baselines in convergence speed and stability, particularly with workers having different numbers of local iterations in their optimizers. BSA is an efficient and stable solution that resolves two critical FL challenges. Its code is openly accessible on GitHub at: https://github.com/dsclinc/FLoP-AG. BSA is compatible with various FL protocols including Federated Average Sag, Federated Push, and Noisy Federated Average Sag. This paper introduces a new class of LCE-based expansions that can be used to tackle any function that can be expressed as the sum of a monotone rearrangement function and another function with known properties in any dimension of 3 or above. To achieve this, our method adapts the techniques of dimension-free bounds that have been established for quantities such as the percolation critical probability and Duffing equation dynamics. This new approach yields precise and simple approximations for functions that are monotone rearrangement-friendly in any number of dimensions. Conversely, it also reveals subtle negative results for functions that exhibit 1-dimensional dependence in multiple ways. This study demonstrates that the concept of monotone rearrangement is a very restrictive one in dimensions of 3 and above, leading to unavoidable biases when working with certain types of function classes in high dimensions. Several concrete examples are provided to illustrate the precision of our method in dimensions of any number of dimensions. To facilitate the use of our method in settings such as statistics and machine learning where functions may have noisy readings, our study also establishes the precise rate at which our approximations converge relative to the noise level in any dimension of 3 or above. To achieve this, our approach adapts the techniques of quantitative Stein's method that have been established for quantities such as the probability distribution of a Brownian motion with drift. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through text prompts have raised hopes for a comparable system driven by visual inputs. We establish key properties of the solution, including its uniqueness and the behavior of its eigenvalues. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of creating an infinite number of distinct Steklov-Robin eigenvalues, a count that matches the number of distinct Dirichlet eigenvalues in a fully rigid square with the same boundary conditions. We also explore an asymptotic representation of the Steklov-Robin eigenvalues and examine the effects of varying the Robin boundary condition on the eigenvalue spectrum. Lastly, we investigate a limiting scenario in which one of the square's edges becomes extremely thin. We show that under this condition, there exists a distinct Steklov-Robin eigenvalue that remains constant, while the other eigenvalues change in a structured manner. Our approach is to view cryptocurrencies as a means of exchange by applying cost consistency theory, which dictates that a suitable exchange medium should be able to cover the costs of its own security and transaction verification processes. We have successfully applied this framework to Bitcoin, thereby demonstrating its status as a reliable exchange medium. This achievement is contingent on the assumption that the values of Bitcoin's issue and transaction verification costs remain stable, a premise that can be evaluated in the future. We have also explored the applicability of our framework to other cryptocurrencies, including Ethereum, Litecoin, and Monero, highlighting the challenges and complexities of doing so. Ultimately, we conclude that these other cryptocurrencies fall short of meeting the criteria set forth by cost consistency theory. We have further modified our framework to consider the concept of persistence in order to assess the likelihood of a cryptocurrency's survival as an exchange medium. This revised theory examines the relationship between a cryptocurrency's issue costs and its current market value, applying it to Bitcoin and other major cryptocurrencies to gauge their potential as long-term exchange mediums. Our analysis of the underlying economics of cryptocurrencies reveals that their viability as exchange mediums is contingent on ongoing and result-driven development and management. We have also applied our concepts of cost consistency and survival to the broader industry as a whole, revealing that the competitive dynamics of the cryptocurrency market have given rise to a self-destructive tendency among its competitors. In contrast, we have found that a cooperative approach, in which the market's cryptocurrencies work together to provide reliable exchange solutions, may ultimately benefit investors and users alike. We believe that our theories provide valuable insights for understanding the present and future of cryptocurrencies. We have further demonstrated the practical utility of our theories by establishing a metric for evaluating a cryptocurrency's market strength, thereby enabling us to forecast the future market share of various cryptocurrencies. Our forecasts, which are based on the long-term survival theories developed in this study, have previously been shared on social media and have proven to be accurate. We have also applied our research to the field of information technology, where we have used our theories to identify areas of the cryptocurrency market that are prime for the disruption of innovative technologies, such as the blockchain 2.0 and 3.0, through the application of artificial intelligence. One of the key factors in successfully transferring objects between robotic arms is manipulability. This paper introduces a novel approach called HRMA to facilitate precise transfer operations between robotic arms. HRMA decouples object and arm movements, allowing these devices to move in optimal trajectories by aligning arm configurations with a predetermined realm. This realm represents a specific region within the arm's workspace, and it can be determined using a robot-specific metric function. To refine the accuracy of HRMA's transfers, HRMA-Aware ICP has been developed as an optimization technique. This method employs an iterative algorithm based on an octree data structure to align the realms of the planning and target arms by iteratively converging on corresponding features. This integration of HRMA and HRMA-Aware ICP has been validated through a series of simulated and real-world experiments, and the results show its superior performance over other transfer and alignment techniques. The major contributions of this research are: (i) HRMA's introduction of a manipulability-based realm transfer protocol, (ii) the development of HRMA-Aware ICP with its unique features and from-surface to surface cost function, and (iii) the demonstration of its performance improvements over other techniques. In a study of Higgs boson pair production, researchers used the NLO QCD matrix element calculation to evaluate the cross-section for the process $pp \to \textrm{HH} + \textrm{X}$, where Higgs bosons decay into $b\bar{b}$ and $WW^*$, and considered $b$-quark pair production as part of the associated background. By incorporating the HH matrix element into an existing generator, the researchers were able to validate the implementation and assess its impact on predicted rates for the Higgs boson pair signal and $b$-quark pair background at the LHC. The addition of the HH matrix element was found to significantly affect the predicted rates at high $p_T$ thresholds, and also influenced the distribution of Higgs pair transverse momentum, although the impact on total rates was found to be relatively small. Specifically, at a 14 TeV LHC with an integrated luminosity of 3000 fb$^{-1}$, the researchers were able to achieve a 10% change in the predicted Higgs pair signal rate. Furthermore, the study found that the incorporation of the HH matrix element led to a 5% change in the predicted $b$-quark pair background rate, and also that the effects of including the HH matrix element in the events were persistent down to $p_T$ thresholds of at least 8 GeV. The researchers noted that the main source of contributions from hard $p_T$ regions in the events came from the matrix element for $b$-quark pair production, rather than the soft radiation component. The study also found that the incorporation of the HH matrix element led to a 10% change in the predicted Higgs pair differential cross-section for its $p_T$ distribution at the LHC. The researchers also looked at the incorporation of the HH matrix element in the $m_{\textrm{HH}}$ distribution and found that this led to a change of around 3%. A common challenge in determining the physical location and orientation of objects in a scene revolves around establishing the relationship between visual properties and physical properties, particularly for objects that move in unpredictable ways. Although advanced computer visions can efficiently detect motion from visual data, transferring this information to physical properties in 3D space remains a significant obstacle due to the complexity of such translations. In real-life situations, precise measurements of rotational velocities are rarely captured; instead, velocities are often expressed in terms of unexpected rotations (e.g., "the ball spun around quickly"). In many cases, video recordings from a single fixed angle can provide valuable insights into the unexpected rotations of moving objects, which in turn facilitate measurements of their 3D positions. In this research, we explore how to utilize observed rotations in unexpected situations to determine the 3D positions of objects, introducing the Unintentional Turntable Problem to achieve this goal. In particular, we design a novel dataset containing more than 30,000 images from over 3000 complex video clips along with corresponding 3D information, which we call the Unintentional Turntables Dataset. In addition, we propose an innovative approach called RotNet that can efficiently learn and accurately identify the rotational velocities of objects in a scene from a single image. Based on the UT-Dataset and through thorough experiments, we demonstrate that it is indeed possible to utilize observed rotations in unexpected situations to determine the 3D positions of objects, outperforming existing methods in this domain. The UT-Dataset and associated software are now available for other researchers at https://rotnet.github.io/utdataset. Furthermore, we provide access to the source code of RotNet at https://rotnet.github.io/. In line with Wikipedia:WikiProject Robotics guidelines, we publicly share the UT-Dataset and RotNet to facilitate further research and enable other researchers to replicate our results. Currently, we are exploring new applications for RotNet and the UT-Dataset, such as utilizing observed rotations in virtual reality environments. Additionally, we are developing new approaches that combine RotNet with other technologies like Reinforcement Learning and 3D Reconstruction for even more accurate 3D estimates. In the near future, we plan to delve into utilizing observed rotations in unexpected situations for estimating the physical properties of objects in a scene, specifically their rotational velocities, and applying these estimates in tasks such as object tracking and state estimation. Despite extensive research on misinformation dissemination via social media, the underlying issue of user interaction with such misinformation remains understudied. This problem is more pronounced in contexts like the COVID-19 vaccine, where direct user engagement has significant real-world implications. This paper presents a novel framework that distinguishes between users accepting or rejecting Twitter posts containing anti-vaccination misinformation. Our proposed approach combines individual user characteristics from historical data with real-time dialogue analysis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this model outperforms existing baseline techniques by a significant margin of 20.88% in identifying acceptance or refusal of misinformation. Notably, our results remain consistent across various experiment configurations. Additionally, we found that users' past behavior on Twitter significantly influences their reaction to misinformation, whereas dialogue features play a more subordinate role in predicting acceptance or refusal. Our findings can inform the development of effective countermeasures against the spread of misinformation. The proposed model, along with experimental data, is openly available on GitHub for reproducibility. This research has been approved by Institutional Review Boards in accordance with ethical standards. Future research can build upon our findings by investigating the self-reported attitudes of Twitter users toward vaccination. Further studies could also explore the application of our proposed framework in other domains of misinformation. Moreover, there are numerous opportunities for incorporating additional features, such as user interactions, to enhance the model's performance. Finally, we suggest examining the potential of our proposed framework in real-world scenarios for mitigating the dissemination of misinformation. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub. This paper addresses the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, focusing on a specific type of solution - those that explode in a specific direction. Initially, we establish conditions for well-defined solutions in the presence of a potential with a well and assume a level of symmetry, reducing the problem to a single equation involving a real variable. Utilizing an energy estimate, we find that under certain criteria, the solutions will not be globally defined. Subsequently, we establish a key inequality, enabling us to demonstrate that in the event of non-existence of minimal solutions, we can derive exploded solutions that exhibit spatial symmetry. Notably, our findings reveal that in the two-dimensional setting, we can guarantee the existence of exploded solutions that exhibit true zero-mode behavior. Lastly, through a combination of energy estimates and maximal principle-based arguments, we demonstrate the existence of exploded solutions in the specific case of the so-called "logarithmic" nonlinearity. To expand their use, researchers reduce the number of nodes in the network.  Different approaches, however, lead to distinct errors and optimal solutions.  This paper introduces Residual Adaptive Node creation Growth, a new method for adjusting the size of the network, and compares it with other approaches using the 1D heat equation and a problem with jumps in solution value.  Additionally, the paper proposes a new error metric that can be used to compare different methods for refining the solution without altering the governing equations.  This error metric is based on the residuals of the solution.  Experiments demonstrate that the new method yields a more accurate solution than other node creation methods and is capable of refining the solution without altering the governing equations.  The new error metric can be used to compare the performance of different methods for refining the solution.  The research indicates that adjusting the size of the network based on the solution's residuals can improve the representation of the solution and reduce the error significantly.  The new approach also allows for the discovery of the solution's initial and boundary conditions from noisy data.  The method outperforms other node creation methods and can be used to adjust the size of CNNs and RNNs in a similar manner.  The code is available at https://github.com/fatiemoussa/RANG. This study examines the behavior and electronic properties of ferroelectric FETs with multiple domains, where the transition between these domains can trigger the negative capacitance effect. We investigate how the negative capacitance response is affected by domain walls and other parameters. Our analysis also considers the impact of domain period and domain orientation on the negative capacitance, as well as the associated energy consumption and variability in these properties. Our findings reveal that the negative capacitance duration and magnitude can be precisely controlled by controlling domain periodicity and orientation. Moreover, we observe that domain orientation variability can lead to instability in the negative capacitance properties, resulting in reduced performance and increased energy consumption. Our study uses a coupled finite element method to simulate the device behavior and electronic transport. We verify the accuracy of our method against existing experimental data and find it to be consistent. Our work provides a thorough understanding of the complex interactions between domain walls, electronic transport, and capacitive response, allowing for the design of stable and high-performance ferroelectric FETs with multi-domain structures. Additionally, we propose a method to achieve variable negative capacitance through the controlled manipulation of domain walls, enabling the development of high-Q and tunable LC circuits. Our study paves the way for the innovative design of electrostatically coupled devices, such as high-speed analog and radio frequency circuits, as well as high-Q and tunable integrated gyrators, oscillators, and filters. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of developing multi-domain ferroelectric FETs with negative capacitance and negative resistance characteristics for high-performance linear transconductor applications. Our analysis considers the effects of variability in domain period and orientation on the negative resistance and transconductor performance. We find that the transconductor gain and bandwidth can be manipulated using period and orientation metrics, as well as temperature-dependent parameters like the oscillator frequency and Q-factor. Our study allows for the identification of design trade-offs between input matching, gain, and bandwidth in multi-domain ferroelectric FETs with negative resistance and negative capacitance. Moreover, we investigate the reliability and variability of ferroelectric FETs with negative capacitance and negative resistance, as well as their performance in integrated transconductor circuits. Our analysis considers various parameters like domain period, orientation, and temperature-dependent properties, as well as the effects of these variables on circuit design and reliability. The increasing complexity of freight systems across North America demands a more sophisticated analysis of their vulnerability. Current research methods focused on freight system fragility rely on detailed simulation-based assessments, but these are often resource-intensive and cannot be scaled back to reveal underlying network structures. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach to create a dependency-fragility insight graph for each node in a freight system. This method enables in-depth analysis of fragility transmission among interdependent components of freight systems. Specifically, our study aims to demonstrate the validity of this approach by mapping the freight network of the Great Lakes region, identifying critical components and disseminating vulnerability throughout the network. Our methodology involves initially defining a freight system's structure and performance metrics, such as service delay and budget impact, as measures of fragility. These metrics are then used to develop a visibility measure, representing the extent of a given node's effect on other nodes in the system. To refine this approach, we apply it to a model of a freight system consisting of 383 nodes and 764 interdependencies. Our results from a coronavirus pandemic-related disruption reveal the spread of vulnerability throughout the network and highlight key components, including freight services, transportation agencies, and shipment operations. Our research offers a novel method for constructing a dependency-fragility insight graph and identifying critical components and vulnerability transmission in freight systems. This approach can be applied to various types of infrastructure and may have implications for policy and practice. Our findings provide a basis for further research on freight system vulnerability and suggest the need for regular assessments of critical component performance and vulnerability transmission. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to research that enhances freight system resilience through a more nuanced understanding of vulnerability transmission. Our method is intended to complement existing freight system assessment methods and we hope that our results will be of value to freight system operators, managers, and policy makers. Our work is a first step in applying the concept of fragility transmission to freight systems and we plan to explore this idea further in future research. Our current findings are a product of desktop research and we aim to collaborate with practitioners and transport stakeholders in the Great Lakes region to refine our approach and test its practicality. Our future work will involve conducting field research to validate our results and make them more relevant to the freight community. Our goal is to make our concept and methods useful and relevant to the freight community and we hope that our results will lead to improved freight system management and policy decisions. Our results provide a basis for future research on freight system vulnerability and we aim to collaborate with transportation stakeholders to apply our concept

Deep learning models like DeepFace and FaceNet have achieved impressive results with their deep convolutional networks, although they have some notable shortcomings. The assumption that facial features are invariant to orientation is not valid for all models, leading to decreased performance when the face orientation is not aligned with the canonical upright position. This is an unsupervised process in DeepFace, resulting in lower accuracy compared to FaceNet. Our research introduces Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs) to replace existing deep convolutional models, eliminating the assumption of orientation invariance. This is achieved by incorporating an additional orientation convolutional module in the initial stages of the network. The proposed OCN architecture outperforms FaceNet and DeepFace in both identification and verification tasks, according to the NIST performance metrics. The results of our experiments indicate that the model's performance improves when the face orientation is aligned, supporting the claim that facial features are not entirely orientation-independent. The 2D FastCNN architecture, responsible for generating the face's low-level features in DeepFace, is replaced with the OCNN to bypass the initial convolutional module. Another deep convolutional model, the OccludedFaceNet, is also reevaluated and replaced with the OCNN to compare their performance under different scenarios. The proposed model's source code and pre-trained models are available for download at the specified URL. Defining uncertainty measurement approaches in machine learning has several benefits, 
such as identifying sources of uncertainty interpretation inconsistencies, 
establishing a common language for uncertainty representation, 
and assessing the performance of uncertainty-based methods.
This work presents a comprehensive overview of current methods for evaluating uncertainty 
and uncertainty-related benchmarks, alongside a newly established framework called 
UncertaintyBenchmark that enables the seamless connection and evaluation of diverse methods. 
Key components of this framework include standardized interfaces for different uncertainty types 
and a comprehensive test suite covering various benchmark datasets, as well as tools 
for comparing competing methods on a unified platform. On this platform, 
the performance of 27 distinct methods for measuring ambiguity has been assessed, 
providing evidence that certain commonly employed methods actually increase ambiguity 
and highlighting open research problems that could be addressed using deep learning. 
Ultimately, the proposed framework seeks to standardize the process of evaluating uncertainty 
and foster collaborative advancement in this area through community engagement and call-to-action.

In this work, we focus on solving the policy improvement problem in impulsive extensive Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) using the Generalized Minimum Residual Method (GMRES). Due to the inherent instability of classic GMRES, we present an alternative iteration scheme, Krylov Approximation Iteration (KAI), based on GMRES. By defining a candidate policy and utilizing the value function, KAI corresponds to a pseudo-policy that can be interpreted as an optimistic reinforcement learning strategy. Notably, both GMRES and KAI are capable of generating intermediately suboptimal policies, which are more accurate than those generated by classic GMRES. Furthermore, under the assumption of finite action spaces, KAI is able to converge to an ε-optimal policy, provided the discount factor is greater than or equal to 0.5. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of KAI in a zero-sum game setting, as well as its comparison with state-of-the-art algorithms such as Model-Based Epicurean and RBAR. Computer simulations producing time series data are often difficult to compare due to varying lengths and values, making direct comparison and ranking a challenging task. This study proposes a new approach to address this issue by dividing each time series into equal segments and evaluating their means. These means are then ranked using a metric score that considers both magnitude and direction. This proposal offers an efficient solution to compare and rank time series data in a comprehensive and standardized way. It demonstrates superiority over traditional comparison metrics in various computer simulation studies by outperforming them in discriminative assessment, improving consistency, and enhancing statistical significance without the need for adjustments. Additionally, this approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of fields. It has been successfully applied in a study on evaluating noise reduction methods for speech enhancement. However, existing methods primarily focus on global corruption and ignore regional corruption patterns that may also affect model robustness. This study introduces regional robustness and explores its potential when targeting both global and regional corruptions. Specific challenges arise when addressing regional corruptions, such as the need to carefully select and combine queries to optimize robustness. Based on this framework, we identify three primary approaches to enhancing model robustness and provide a theoretical justification for each: combining multiple meta-objectives, combining different types of corruption, and utilizing regional queries in the query loop. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods on tabular data and tabular data with relational schemas. Our findings show that regional benefits are contingent upon the specific corruption pattern and depend on various factors, and our proposed methods achieve superior performance in enhancing model robustness. Specifically, our method achieves a relative gain of $0.7\times 10^{-3}$ in relative error reduction on the covertype dataset compared to state-of-the-art methods. we developed a stochastic autoencoder, incorporating noise to counteract
overfitting and generate synthetic spectra in feature space. The model's
generative ability allows it to model various explosion conditions and generate
spectral sequences for individual SN Ia events. Our primary objective is to
investigate the applicability of this autoencoder in learning the intrinsic
properties of SN Ia events. The model is trained using a combination of real and
mock datasets with 348 type Ia supernovae, and its validity is verified by
generating synthetic spectra for unseen SN Ia events, as well as through a
generative latent space analysis. The results indicate that our autoencoder
efficiently captures the intrinsic variability of SN Ia spectra, and given its
good performance, this approach can serve as a useful tool for future studies
on SN Ia cosmological baryon acoustic oscillations and other applications.
Furthermore, our approach provides a useful framework for other astronomical
objects that involve intrinsically variable objects with multiple measurement
time-sequences. The code used for this study is publicly available at this

Understanding the spread of epidemics within complex networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the process, neglecting the potential for group infections. To address this, hypergraphs offer a more comprehensive framework to model these interactions. We introduce a new limit to measure the likelihood of an epidemic spreading through a hypergraph: the extinction probability $\lambda_{\max}$. In this study, we explore the applicability of this new framework on two levels. Firstly, we evaluate the effect of adding new edges to existing graphs, revealing that the addition of new edges never worsens the extinction probability. Secondly, we analyze a model where new interactions are introduced randomly, finding that the resulting extinction probability converges to a Gaussian distribution as the number of edges increases. These findings validate the use of the new framework, offering a more accurate assessment of the conditions under which an epidemic transmits through group transmissions. We further substantiate these claims using real-world examples, such as the transmission of measles in London and the spread of COVID-19 among passengers on the Diamond Princess cruise ship, applying our framework to these instances to measure the impact of group transmissions on the likelihood of an epidemic spreading. In particular, we find that the consideration of non-pairwise interactions significantly raises the likelihood of an epidemic spreading in certain scenarios, underlining the importance of modeling these interactions in epidemiological modeling. Finally, we propose the development of future research, suggesting the application of our framework to the study of various epidemics and the exploration of other models of interacting graphs. The rapid dissemination of misinformation through mass messaging services like WhatsApp poses significant challenges, particularly during major global events. To combat this issue, WhatsApp introduced limitations on mass forwarding to slow the spread of potentially harmful content. To assess the effectiveness of these limitations, we developed a custom WhatsApp client that allows users to circumvent the restrictions. Utilizing this tool, we launched an experiment designing two types of messages: one containing purely fictional information and the other based on real news. Both were disseminated within a closed user group to exclude external recipients. Our analysis shows that, prior to the introduction of limitations, the fictional message reached a significantly larger group size. Conversely, the group receiving the other message increased in size after the limitations were implemented. Building on these findings, we created a mathematical model simulating the dissemination of misinformation through a network. Our model suggests that the sudden surge in misinformation spread, observed before the limitations were introduced, can be attributed to a combination of high information quality and a large number of initial recipients. Furthermore, we verified that the solution to our mathematical model closely mirrors the results from our large-scale experiment. Our study demonstrates the ineffectiveness of simply limiting mass forwarding to address the complex issue of misinformation spread. Instead, our work presents several promising research directions for further exploration. Specifically, we highlight the potential importance of understanding the origins of the initial forward and distinguishing between reliable and unreliable information to address the challenge at hand. Furthermore, we suggest that these investing methods are better suited to underperforming asset managers seeking to differentiate themselves from the rest, thereby potentially increasing their market share. A beneficial approach for updating machine learning models while respecting data privacy exists in federated learning. This method allows models to be refined using client data and maintaining client data confidentiality. This work explores a novel application of federated learning to audio classification, particularly for datasets with and without label information. When labels are present, conventional federated learning can be applied, but it requires clients to share their model or gradient information, which may violate privacy due to potential model representation leakage. On the other hand, when labels are absent, as in the case with a Novel Categories Zero-Shot Classification dataset, a possible solution involves sharing centroids with clients by the server. However, the current challenge lies in synchronizing local and server models without knowing which data the clients have selected for training. This issue has been addressed by proposing local updates that generalize across different datasets, which can then be safely shared on the server. Additionally, the server model updates are enabled through an averaging process of shared vectors. This approach was tested using the OpenMic federated learning dataset and Novel Categories Zero-Shot Classification dataset, with the results showing its effectiveness and outperforming performance over baseline models. Recent research on high-dimensional quantum entanglement has made significant advancements, but current experiments are restricted by limited detection capabilities. Our method's effectiveness was demonstrated in two scenarios: specific helium-3 centerline laser illumination and broadband illumination, each resulting in a distinct error mechanism. Furthermore, CTP enabled accurate purification measurement in a scenario where traditional methods experienced difficulties due to spectral distortion. Our study provides a practical solution to the common problem of decoherence in quantum physics experiments. Specifically, our proposal's focus on GHZ states, although exemplary, can be applied to a broader range of entangled states. This study analyzes COVID-19 reporting by 250 top-rated news outlets in the U.S., focusing on coverage disparities across regions, timing, and audience segments. It finds that news outlets initially covered COVID-19 sporadically but later reported it regularly, with variations depending on region, ownership, and audience. While many news outlets received low traffic, some owned by Heritage, Gannett, and Scripps received above average traffic for their respective regions. Interestingly, progressive news outlets covered COVID-19 more frequently than conservative ones, but with fewer articles overall. When comparing news outlets' coverage to actual COVID data, a positive correlation was found to exist locally and regionally. Lastly, it was discovered that liberal and progressive news outlets covered COVID-19 more extensively than conservative ones in many regions, but with some exceptions. These patterns hold true when considering the perspective of readers rather than news producers. To mitigate the influence of confounding variables, a range of techniques including those not previously reported in news research were employed. These findings suggest that news coverage may be shaped by a complex interplay of factors, including the characteristics of news outlets and their audiences, as well as the severity of COVID-19 outbreaks in respective regions. These results could be of great use to policymakers and researchers. To facilitate reproduction of these results, the data and analysis code have been shared publicly, enabling other researchers to build upon these findings. Suggestions for future research are presented, with a particular focus on the causes and consequences of news coverage disparities. These ideas involve statistical modeling techniques not previously applied to news research, as well as data sets comprising COVID-related news articles from even more extensive set of outlets, covering an even longer time period. These additional data sets comprise news content from over 500 top-rated outlets, spanning from January 2020 to June 2021. Furthermore, the influence of COVID-19 coverage on public perceptions and behaviors has been left unexplored in this study and remains a subject for future research, as well as the potential long-term implications of news coverage disparities on public health and the information ecosystem. To address these questions and investigate the long-term effects of news coverage disparities, a new dataset is being prepared, consisting of COVID-related news articles from over 500 top-rated outlets, spanning from early 2020 to late 2021. This new dataset will permit analysis of how news coverage of COVID-19 has developed over time and enable examination of the potential long-term implications of news coverage disparities on public health and the information ecosystem. A new class of lossless and approximate membership filters called xor filters is introduced, incorporating elements of Bloom filters but offering enhanced efficiency. Specifically, a single universal hash function is required for each element in a filter, as opposed to multiple hash functions needed for insertion and query operations in traditional Bloom filters. This simplification results in faster insertion and deletion processes, while maintaining similar query times. Furthermore, a proposed implementation of xor filters demonstrates better storage efficiency compared to Bloom filters with the same false positive rates. Moreover, a novel approximate reverse filter technique is developed, enabling the identification of approximate members within a specified fraction of the original set with substantially reduced computation time. Numerical simulations have demonstrated the advantages of xor filters over both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in terms of processing speed and memory utilization. Interestingly, a notable observation from the results is the more significant storage efficiency of xor filters over Bloom filters, even at low utilization levels, which is unlike the expected outcome. A detailed analysis of this phenomenon is also presented in the research. Overall, xor filters have been found to be an attractive alternative due to their faster insertion, deletion, and membership verification capabilities, as well as better storage efficiency, especially when the false positive rate is low. Additionally, their compactness has been enhanced by reducing the storage needed for a given false positive rate. With these advantages, xor filters are expected to be more suitable for various high-performance applications over traditional Bloom filters. This work presents FLVoogd, a robust and confidential federated learning framework. Current FL techniques are susceptible to attacks such as data poisoning and model poisoning. Moreover, they raise concerns for data owners' privacy as their data is shared with potential adversaries. FLVoogd addresses these challenges via introduction of a reliable server and trustworthy client relationship built on blockchain technology, as well as leveraging VGGNet's feature-extraction properties to maintain participants' data and model confidentiality. Evaluations performed on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FLVoogd in providing resilient and private federated learning solutions. Additionally, the framework exhibits comparable accuracy to existing FL methods while significantly reducing model updating frequency. Experimental results of data and model poisoning attacks on FLVoogd reveal a robust performance with minimal server and client vulnerability. Furthermore, FLVoogd's anonymity preserves participants' privacy, outperforming existing FL methods. Investigation of the impact of blockchain-related parameters on FLVoogd's performance also provides valuable insights for future research. A key obstacle in developing autonomous vehicles lies in transferring learning from simulated to real-world environments. Current methods, which evaluate policy by assessing predicted actions with actual actions taken in a simulated setting, fall short in translating skills to real-world settings, primarily due to their failure to account for variations in scene context between simulations and reality. Conversely, directly training models in real-world settings is impractical without adequate resources and time. Our novel approach addresses this issue by having a simulated network predict gradient information from map data and a real-world/non-real-world classifier to determine scene context, whereas the real-world network generates actual image content. Furthermore, our method uses a novel shared-policy architecture, allowing the same network to perform both simulated and real-world predictions. Our method effectively closes the sim2real gap for end-to-end navigation, yielding performance comparable to state-of-the-art human-level benchmarks in real-world settings. Specifically, our navigation capabilities achieve success rates of 95.54% for walking and 94.17% for driving. Our code and demo are publicly available. Deepfake videos, particularly those created using generative adversarial networks (GANs), have become a rising concern due to their potential for causing harm through the spread of false information. Unlike text-based deepfakes, such as deep learning-based language models, image and video deepfakes have seen more implementation in practical applications. Our study differs from other research by focusing on the limitations of current deepfake detection techniques, revealing their inability to effectively spot strong deepfakes in real-world settings. We propose a new approach for creating more convincing strong deepfakes and, concurrently, a strong deepfake detection method through an improved deepfake classification network. Our work contrasts with existing research by performing create-and-detect experiments, highlighting the need for further novel methods against sophisticated deepfakes. Our analysis demonstrates the efficacy of our method in successfully identifying previously unseen, highly realistic deepfakes, achieving an 88% success rate in create-and-detect tests. Combining it with advanced computer simulations of star formation and evolution enables us to assess the roles of different processes in shaping the properties and compositions of dwarf galaxies. This supports the theory that this process played a significant role in shaping the properties of dwarf galaxies. Finally, we've found that the galaxy M81d, which is part of the Hubble Space Telescope's Legacy From Space project, is composed of gas with a metal content significantly higher than typical for its distance. We develop a dual transformation for the restricted MDP and propose the Primary-Dual Repeated Sarsa (PDRS) algorithm to solve this formulation. The PDRS algorithm has several key benefits, including being implemented without the need for a Markov evolution model, being applicable to infinite-horizon problems with discounted rewards and average reward contexts, and providing a straightforward method for calculating the optimal value function and action choices. Moreover, the PDRS algorithm has been found to be a robust and efficient solver in a variety of experimental scenarios. Both theoretical and practical research on this topic has made significant progress in recent years, and this research aims to contribute to this effort by exploring the concept of using layered navigation controllers for underwater vehicles. These controllers, inspired by bird flight patterns, offer an appealing alternative to the traditional balanced force-based navigation method commonly used in autonomous aircraft. Although the latter approach ensures stability and predictable behavior, it may not be the most efficient choice for underwater vehicles due to its high computational demands. In contrast, the layered controller is expected to require less computational power, making it more suitable for vehicles equipped with basic navigation systems such as a single compass sensor. To further enhance the robustness of the layered controller, this research focuses on developing a real-time sonar integration module that utilizes a unique interpolation technique to rapidly detect and identify obstacles within the vehicle's surroundings. The result is a significant improvement in processing speed, up to 2.5 times faster, compared to a conventional sonar algorithm. The integrated system, comprising both the layered controller and the optimized sonar module, has been successfully tested in various simulated and real-world underwater environments to verify its efficacy and robustness. Our findings also show that techniques like Correlated Cluster Analysis and Bicluster Analysis fail to effectively handle existing-absisting data, while methods like Stochastic Gradient Descent and Lee and Hwang's method may struggle with positive data constraints. Computed Tomography (CT) is widely used in radiology to diagnose and treat patients, particularly for internal problems such as cardiovascular disease, tumors, and body scans. However, older CT scanners have limitations such as poor high-energy measurement capabilities. This leads to poor image quality at deeper levels, affecting diagnosis. Recent studies have proposed using electronic portability to obtain multiple energy levels, but the resulting data is subject to noise. This project aims to develop a complete reconstruction process, incorporating patient density and movement, external noise and variability in measurement. Our solution involves an iterative process that begins with an initial measurement correction, followed by a non-convex variational approach that produces accurate images at various energy levels. Our results show that our method can handle noisy data and demonstrate significant improvements over traditional techniques. Furthermore, our framework can be adapted for automatic tissue type identification and estimating tissue water and dry components. Our study confirms that our method can produce accurate results at various energy levels. Our code is available online for public use. This study was funded by Zebra Medical Technologies. Z. A novel technique has been devised for merging three distinct types of de facto ab initio computational methods used in nuclear physics: those based on in-medium similarity renormalization group, excitation spectrum embedding, and generative neural network techniques. This merger can accommodate a wide range of interactions, even those with significant long-range characteristics. Furthermore, the merged framework's structure allows for efficient calculation of ground states and 1-body and 2-body correlation functions. As a proof of concept, a fully computational model of the deuteron and an integrated model of the double-beta decay channel in 16K have been created. Results from these calculations match experimental data with high precision when compared to isospin-symmetric Argonne potentials. The merged approach's potential applications include multi-particle reactions and decay studies as well as the detailed analysis of correlation structures in nuclei. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly benefits from using array-based programming, especially when dealing with massive data. Despite the performance boost, array-based programs on CPUs or GPUs often experience slow memory access due to frequent and random memory allocations, leading to significant performance losses. Current GPU memory allocators have notable shortcomings, including inefficient, overlapping memory blocks, biased towards CPUs, that fail to consider the unique access patterns of array-based programs on GPUs. To address these shortcomings, we introduce DynaSOAr, a novel, highly efficient memory allocator designed for array-based programs, optimized to run concurrently on GPUs. DynaSOAr incorporates several innovative features, including a size-based partitioning scheme, a dynamic size array, and a size-optional linked list, all of which aim to optimize memory allocation and free operations to match the actual memory usage patterns of array-based programs. By doing so, DynaSOAr enhances memory efficiency, reduces memory allocation and access competition, and consequently leads to notable performance improvements, with memory allocation and array access speed-ups of up to 30x and 20x, respectively, in practical use cases. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's innovative design allows it to remain independent of specific programming frameworks, making it highly versatile and easily integratable into existing code. To demonstrate its efficiency, we show DynaSOAr outperforming other state-of-the-art allocators in array-based programs, such as OpenACC and OpenCL, by a significant margin, further solidifying its potential as a leading memory allocator for array-based programs on GPUs. Finally, we showcase the success of DynaSOAr in a real-world application, where it results in a 10x performance improvement over the SOA version of a well-known scientific program, further solidifying its potential as a leading solution for practical use cases. Related source code is publicly accessible on GitHub, reference number 801247, and our future plans involve integrating DynaSOAr with existing GPU programming frameworks, such as CUDA, HIP, OpenACC, OpenCL, and MIOVI. We are also exploring new directions to extend DynaSOAr's functionality to match the actual memory usage patterns of array-based programs on GPUs. We anticipate these efforts to extend DynaSOAr's lead in efficiency and performability. We will make these findings available soon. It is worth mentioning that DynaSOAr does not have any political, social or financial limitations, as it falls under the permissive BSD-3 license. We are also investigating the possibility of making DynaSOAr widely accessible

We have found that when these two components are subjected to a linear load, a new type of sound wave, characterized by a unique displacement field, emerges in the low-frequency regime. Furthermore, this sound wave propagates at a speed determined by the effective sound velocity of the entangled condensate. In the absence of spin-orbit coupling, the sound wave frequency exhibits a quadratic dependence on the wave number, whereas a linear dependence is observed when the spin-orbit coupling is present. Our findings, derived from the extension of the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation to the context of spin liquids, are applicable to both two and three-dimensional systems. A partial arrangement within this structure refers to a collection of non-intersecting lines, and a neighbor-transitive set is a subset of the structure's elements exhibiting neighbor-preservation and transitivity. This paper delves into the construction and examination of neighbor-transitive sets in quadrangles, focusing on their associated neighbor-transitive codes and the relationship between partial arrangements, their automorphism groups, and incidence properties in the context of Delsarte vectors and neighbor-transitive codes. In addition to general results, this paper specifically analyses neighbor-transitive sets in the quadrangles derived from odd-dimensional projective spaces, hemisystems of finite spherical codes, and hemisystems of finite Hermitian codes. It also proves a long-standing conjecture regarding the neighbor-transitive code of quadrangles in the generalized hexagon. This research further presents an open problem and partially answers another conjecture. The paper is divided into three sections, with Appendix A and Bibliography included. Section 1 introduces the necessary background and key concepts, while Section 2 constructs and examines neighbor-transitive sets in specific quadrangles and their associated code properties. Section 3 discusses the automorphism groups of partial arrangements and incidence properties in the context of Delsarte vectors and neighbor-transitive codes. Finally, Appendix A provides supplementary information and a counterexample in support of a particular conjecture. This paper concludes with a comprehensive bibliography. This research presents a novel and efficient technique for word translation that leverages large parallel datasets that are often not perfectly aligned. Our method avoids the typical requirement for paired sentence data by using an unsupervised alignment approach based on multiple outside sources of bilingual data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique using a sample dataset of sentence pairs from the Wiktionary database. This resource is extensive and readily available for many language pairs, encompassing over 37 million sentence pairs in over 200 language pairs. Our results show that our method achieves a high accuracy for mapping words in foreign languages to their English equivalents, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods that utilize sentence-based paired data. We also show that our method can be applied in real-time to establish word translations based on an analysis of its categorical components. This research could enable a range of translation applications, including real-time and on-the-fly translation services. One potential use case is a virtual assistant traveling to a foreign country that wants to understand menu items or know where something is. Another example is a search engine that can provide search results in a user's native language even if the terms are unfamiliar. Additionally, this research could enhance the functionality of language learning apps by providing users with a better understanding of words in a foreign language. It could also be utilized by a business traveler to decipher unfamiliar Japanese restaurant menus or a historian researching texts in an unfamiliar language. The code for this research is available on a public repository. Evaluation results demonstrate the superiority of our method over other approaches, such as bilingual word embeddings and word embeddings that can be translated, in terms of accuracy for a given word in a foreign language when paired with its corresponding English word. This is a notable finding because previous research in this area used sentence-based paired data, a resource that is often imperfectly aligned and difficult to obtain for low-resource language pairs. Our method instead utilizes large parallel datasets that are available for many language pairs, a resource that includes the extensive dataset from the Wiktionary database. This research also presents a sample dataset of sentence pairs from the Wiktionary database, a resource that includes over 37 million sentence pairs in over 200 language pairs. We also show that our method can be applied in real-time and that its accuracy can be predicted based on the characteristics of the words involved. We propose a distorted resolvent method to obtain Nash equilibria for static Nash games and discrete-time stochastic Nash games with short horizons. Our approach involves three key components: a distorted resolvent that reverses the nonmonotone monotone operator theory, a continuous-time perturbed dynamic system that yields stable trajectories, and a small perturbation size that ensures reasonable game outcomes. Unlike existing large perturbation methods, our method can generate precise equilibrium trajectories without sacrificing economic significance. Additionally, our analysis includes rigorous estimates of the perturbation size and validation of the distorted resolvent theory. We apply our method to three exemplary modeling scenarios: a follower's game involving linear time-invariant systems with quadratic costs, and two stochastic zero-sum games involving linear Schr\"{o}dinger equations and matrix $M$-matrices. Our results not only provide theoretical insights but also offer practical tools for generating Nash equilibria. Our approach is best viewed as a three-part distillation of the nonmonotone monotone operator theory, the perturbed dynamic system, and the stochastic Nash games with the perturbation size serving as a switch that separates the stable trajectories from the equilibrium paths. In this study, we introduce the dissipative Combined Dark Model (CDM) by incorporating a perfect fluid and a cosmological constant into the combined dark energy/scalar-waves framework. We then derive the field equations for the framework in the presence of a perfect fluid, and apply the quadratic variational perturbation method to investigate cosmological perturbations. Our analysis of the background dynamics reveals that the CDM model adheres to the acceleration-equation result derived from the Friedmann equations. We also found that the scalar perturbation grows at a rate of $k/a$, where $k$ is the wavenumber and $a$ is the scale factor. However, the vector and tensor perturbations follow the equations of motion dictated by the Lagrange multiplier. Furthermore, our investigation of the matter power spectrum as a function of scale reveals a decrease in power, and observed the breakdown of the Hubble flow at a specific scale, known as the matter-dominated era. We further modified the CDM model to include a interaction term, and applied the acceleration-equation result and scaling-law result to derive constraints on the interaction parameter $\lambda$. We then applied the matter power spectrum with interactions to model deviations from $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, and used the SDSS data to obtain an upper limit on the interaction parameter $\lambda$ of 0.0632. Finally, our investigation of the matter power spectrum as a function of scale in the interacting CDM model reveals a decrease in power at small scales, and observed that the matter power spectrum is shifted relative to the $\Lambda$CDM model at large scales. We demonstrated that the magnitude of this shift is dependent on the interaction parameter $\lambda$. We further extended the investigation of the matter power spectrum to the galaxy number count, and used the dataset from the SDSS to obtain an upper limit on the interaction parameter $\lambda$ of 0.0623. We also analyzed the behavior of the interaction parameter $\lambda$ as a function of scale in the galaxy number count, and observed that the interaction parameter is not zero at small scales. We further estimated the interaction parameter $\lambda$ from the dataset of the Planck 2015 likelihood file, and found that the interaction parameter is between 0.0623 and 0.0632. We also investigated whether the interaction parameter $\lambda$ is sufficient to explain the 'coincidence problem', and found that the time scale at which matter and dark energy densities are equal is between 0.043 and 0.046.

Although this outcome aligns with existing research, our approach is distinct from previous studies. This technique has the potential for adaptation to higher-dimensional scenarios. Generative diffusion models have achieved notable success in generating semantic images and improving real-image enhancement, but their training often relies on unsupervised image manipulation which can be inconsistent with specific creative goals. This work bridges this gap by introducing a novel steady-state creator framework that incorporates semantic guidance at the diffusion level, leveraging the diffusion process's iterative nature to fuse multiple guidance signals. Unlike prior approaches, our creator framework offers a unified Latent-Space perspective, allowing for the joint optimization of multiple guidance signals. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in generating images that adhere to precise semantic standards while producing high-quality, varied, and realistic outputs. Our creator framework also outperforms state-of-the-art models in semantic image synthesis and unsupervised object removal tasks. Furthermore, we unlock new applications by extracting semantically coherent states from the latent space, enabling efficient semantic image manipulation through generative flow. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/fatemehkabir/Steady-Creator. Our demo video can be found on Vimeo at https://vimeo.com/446589477.

BNNs' ability to provide accurate predictions, reliable uncertainty estimates, and robustness against distribution shifts is key to the universal steganalysis of embedded images.
