In brain tissue, the regulation of substance transport is vital to maintaining proper cellular function, particularly in areas like the brain's hippocampus and cerebral cortex, where the process is critical for learning and memory. Unlike passive diffusion, active transport can move substances against concentration gradients by using energy, but it also has limitations and can become overwhelmed by high delivery rates, leading to blocked transport and ultimately cellular damage. To investigate this "transport congestion" more effectively, we're developing a mathematical model that incorporates the biological mechanisms of substance transport, regulation, and congestion. This model will help us simulate substance movement and identify the mechanisms that protect cells against congestion and the effects of substance removal. By optimizing parameters in a way that minimizes congestion-based damage to cells, the model can also generate predictive scenarios for understanding the consequences of failed transport mechanisms and the benefits of therapeutic interventions. This abstract summarizes our research, focusing on the development and application of a novel optimality condition that arises from our model. It has implications for the broader theory of optimal control, yet it also has practical significance for the fields of neuroscience and neuroengineering. Furthermore, we use our model to illustrate the interconnectedness of substance transport, brain function, and the functioning of specific brain structures, such as the temporal lobe and the brainstem. This model serves as a tool for communicating with neuroscientists and neuroengineers working in these fields. Finally, we highlight the model's flexibility and highlight specific examples of parameter values that can help us better understand the effects of variable brain blood flow and the movement of substances assisted by carriers. These scenarios include models of compounded transport mechanisms and transport models that take into account the unique properties of the substance itself. These scenarios can inform future research into the molecular biology of substance transport. Ultimately, we aim to use our model to investigate the relationship between substance transport and memory, but we begin by examining a simpler parameter optimization problem. This problem involves finding the best transport settings to minimize congestion and maintain proper cellular function during periods of normal activity, but we also explore the what-if scenarios of altered transport parameters and the effects of blocked transport mechanisms. This optimization problem is particularly relevant because it allows us to investigate the most effective transport settings to maintain proper cellular function during normal activity, but we also explore the challenges of adapting to changing conditions, such as when substances are delivered at very high rates. This research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. Yet, due to turbulence in three-body semileptonic decay processes, predicting the resulting hadronic parton distribution is particularly challenging. In this study, we introduce a scheme to calculate the hadronic parton distribution of three-body semileptonic $\tau$ meson decays while also developing corresponding representation theories for the $\U(3)$ and $\U(2)$ gluon distribution matrices. Additionally, we establish a set of unitary coefficients that facilitate the calculation of the hadronic parton distribution. Using this method, we derive the parton distribution for the resonance $h_1(1600)$ and demonstrate how to calculate shape factors in three-body semileptonic $\tau$ meson decays. Our proposed scheme is compared against existing data and theoretical predictions. Given its reliance on experimental data for initialization, we find notable agreement with current observations. Furthermore, we explore the role of Fock space in three-body semileptonic $\tau$ meson decays, revealing how it governs the distribution of the $\tau$ meson in its various decay states. Our work offers a novel, yet straightforward, approach to describing the parton distribution in three-body semileptonic $\tau$ meson decays. This method, characterized by its density matrix calculations and unitary coefficient calculations, demonstrates that the parton distribution is essentially a manifestation of the $\U(3)$ or $\U(2)$ gluon distribution matrix. Our study also highlights the importance of initializing the density matrix with appropriate coefficients, which are subsequently modified through unitary coefficient calculations. In this respect, we successfully applied our method to predict the parton distribution of several resonances, including $h_1(1600)$, $h_2(2895)$, and $h_3(1720)$. Our study also explores three-body non-relativistic $\tau$ meson decays, revealing a new approach to calculating shape factors. This method, characterized by its density matrix calculations and unitary coefficient calculations, demonstrates not only system-dependent symmetry but also its inherent density matrix nature. Our study further reveals that although relativistic $\tau$ meson decays exhibit complex three-body turbulence, relativistic corrections do not significantly alter the parton distribution. Recent advancements in motion deblurring have been significantly facilitated by deep learning techniques. However, existing models can only directly learn movement-related information or gain insight from a separate auxiliary network. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called Pseudo-Blur Generator (PBG), which enables a more efficient training process for deep learning models through data augmentation. The PBG method creates synthetic blurs on input images to simulate actual motion effects, producing clearer images even in challenging scenarios. The proposed PBG method streamlines the training process for a single model to improve its performance across various blur types and intensities. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the PBG method, yielding better outcomes than current state-of-the-art models in terms of objective metrics and subjective quality assessments. Our analysis involves finding an upper limit for this eigenvalue through a nonlinear optimization problem with monotone operators, resulting in a more accurate estimate than previously known limits. The reasoning employs new approaches and concepts, such as the Fenchel-Euler-Lagrange decomposition and the concavity of the operator's Lagrangian. The discussion is supplemented by examples and a companion paper, which aims to apply these findings to ground states in nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equations. The proposed methods also shed light on the relations between the eigenvalues of linearized problems and the first eigenvalue of the negative Laplacian with a Robin boundary condition. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant attention in processing complex graph data. However, the theoretical foundation of GCNNs remains unclear, particularly regarding the matching of the network's filtering effect with the graph's localized smoothing filter. This phenomenon is referred to as an illusion. The GCNN's filtering effect resembles a semi-convex kernel that blurs graph inputs, but it lacks a definitive theoretical basis. The current approaches attempt to link GCNNs with various graph signal processing (GSP) techniques, but these attempts fail to explicitly derive the matching filter and the corresponding semi-convex kernel. This research aims to address the ambiguity surrounding GCNNs' theoretical foundation by introducing a novel method to explicitly match the GCNN's filtering effect with the localized smoothing filter. The proposed method employs the inverse multi-channel matched filter (MmF) to match the GCNN's filtering effect with the localized smoothing filter. The MmF's weight matrix provides a direct and concrete connection between GCNNs and the graph's localized smoothing filter, but it is limited in its ability to derive the semi-convex kernel of the forward GCNN model. An alternative method, the normal equation-based matching filter (NmF), is introduced to match the GCNN's filtering effect with the localized smoothing filter. The NmF's normal equation successfully links GCNNs with the graph's localized smoothing filter, but it is hindered by an infinite series of the graph's semi-convex kernel. An explicit derivation of the GCNN's semi-convex kernel is elusive, but it is conjectured that the graph's semi-convex kernel can be effectively approximated through the graph's personalized PageRank (PPR) technique. The PPR is a well-known method that is closely related to the graph's localized smoothing filter, but it is not considered a direct derivation of the semi-convex kernel. The PPR's connection with GCNNs is explored through an empirical analysis of the matching filters' weight matrices under different training and testing scenarios. The results reveal that the PPR is an excellent predictor of the GCNN's semi-convex kernel, but further research is needed to establish a theoretical basis for this observation. In conclusion, this research addresses the ambiguity surrounding GCNNs' theoretical foundation by introducing a novel method to explicitly match the GCNN's filtering effect with the localized smoothing filter. The match between GCNNs and the graph's localized smoothing filter is achieved through the MmF's weight matrix

This paper introduces a novel approach called Profound Contextualized Self Learning (ProCSL), a contextualized dependency parsing technique developed specifically for languages that have limited resources. It incorporates elements of contextualized models, self-supervised learning, and stack-affecting mechanisms to effectively capture long-distance relationships, contextualized dependencies, and contextualized syntax. We implemented ProCSL on four low-resource languages (-Egyptian Arabic, Swahili, Javanese, and Tagalog) and compared its performance with leading resource-rich models, as well as a leading modern dependency parsing model, by evaluating its accuracy on various metrics. The results showed that ProCSL consistently outperformed the other models in almost all the metrics on these four languages, achieving an average increase of 2.07% in F-score. Moreover, our model improved the already strong UPOS tagging in CoNLL-Drop by 1.01%. Notably, our model's performance on languages with previously established treebank data (like Egyptian Arabic and Swahili) surpassed the F-score by 2.54% and 3.64% respectively. On languages without any established treebank data (like Javanese and Tagalog), our model's performance surpassed the F-score by 4.34% and 3.61% respectively. The code and model artifacts are available for public use at the link provided. Additionally, the treebank enhancements we created for Egyptian Arabic, Swahili, Javanese, and Tagalog can be found on the NLP Accordion platform. We are also planning to extend our work on Tagalog to include the analysis of contextualized dependencies. The current research has significant practical implications for applications such as machine translation, summarization, and text-based chat in low resource settings. Lastly, our model has the potential to be adapted in various other natural language tasks that rely on contextualized models. Cai, Furer, and Immerman demonstrated that NP problems can be solved by a class of problems solvable in nondeterministic logarithmic time with a specific limitation - the amount of time for which some parts of the input can be predicted. In this study, the initial limitation is relaxed to investigate the impact on the class of solvable problems. In particular, the class of decision problems with polynomial duration (PD) is examined, where solutions for any given input can be produced within a certain fixed amount of time, and this amount of time does not affect the results. The study shows that each decision problem with a polynomial duration that belongs to the NP class can be solved using a more restricted version of the Cai-Furer-Immerman (CFI) class of graphs, where certain limited time constraints apply. Additionally, this research establishes a significant relationship between the PD class and CFI graphs, and it proves a long-standing conjecture that PD is equal to CFI. The proof involves creating a network with specific properties for any given decision problem with a polynomial duration. In doing so, this research advances the understanding of such problems by giving them a more limited but still flexible representation within a more restricted class of graphs. Furthermore, this research introduces a new d-step symmetric network, where solutions can be found within a specific duration, and shows that any decision problem with a polynomial duration (and a certain other constraint) can be solved using a more restricted version of this class of graphs. In doing so, this research demonstrates that the class of one-directional CFI graphs is not sufficient to solve all decision problems with a polynomial duration, and this result holds for other related classes of graphs. Lastly, this research presents a more limited but still flexible alternative to the CFI class of graphs, where solutions can be found within a certain time with some predictions, and shows that this new class contains all decision problems with a polynomial duration. In doing so, this research proves a long-standing conjecture that PD is equal to CFI. The full text of this research appears in a separate paper. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes a metal-insulator transformation when contaminated with oxygen. This unique property, coupled with the presence of competing phases, Eu2+ and Bi3+, leads to unpredictable electrical conductivity. To comprehend the alteration in conductivity, we applied hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy and performed first-principles calculations on (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7. These studies show that Bi ions replace Eu ions near the surface, while remaining stoichiometric deep within the sample. This analysis also identifies weakly bound electrons on the surface, attributed to Bi ions, whereas deep within the sample, we find typical Mott insulator characteristics. This self-consistent model governs the entire series and the driving force behind the insulator-to-conductor transition is the bi-ion's unique potential. This discovery paves the way for further research into insulator-to-conductor transformations. Lastly, we explore the potential for Weyl semimetal formation within the series. 

In order to gain a deeper understanding of this process, we used XPS on several samples from the series, including (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 with 0 <= x <= 1. The results from these measurements revealed the presence of electrons near the Fermi level on the Eu surface, whereas deep within the sample, we measured Ir 4f peaks. This indicated that Bi ions cause chemical doping on the Eu surface, resulting in weakly bound electrons near the Fermi level. The shift in Bi 4f peaks towards lower binding energies suggests that Bi ions have replaced Eu ions on the surface, a phenomenon supported by our first-principles calculations. The Bi ions on the surface have a potential of 0.53 eV, significantly higher than the average potential of 0.13 eV deep within the sample. This potential variation is the primary driver of electron potential at the Fermi level, causing the metal-insulator transition. The surface Bi potential also results in a 0.30/Bi concentration change in electron potential at the Fermi level. This effect is the primary reason for the series' insulator-to-conductor transition and the Weyl semimetal's potential formation. The depth of our samples was then examined using cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy, revealing that Bi ions had replaced Eu ions on the surface, while deep within the sample, we measured 10-30 nm stoichiometric layers. This paper explores the concept of circular and nontransitive likelihoods, extending the idea of nontransitive dice, where the outcome of one die is always higher than another's, but not necessarily higher than a third's. We show that these likelihoods can be represented as probability measures over circular or linear ordered spaces, and present specific examples, such as the von Mises distribution, in which the ordering is based on angle in a circle. We go on to demonstrate that any circular likelihood can be reinterpreted as a linear likelihood with a specific 'tail' weighting. We also present an algorithm for determining whether a given likelihood is circular or not. We find that our experiments using data from Kaggle competitions reveal that the likelihood being circular is not uncommon, and that this property can provide a basis for feature selection. Finally, we touch on the implications of our findings for decision-making, where the conventional ordering of options, based on their likelihoods, may not always be the best choice. This raises the broader question of whether it is always desirable to prefer options with higher likelihoods in decision theory. We propose calling this preference'standard' and distinguishing between it and the concept of standardness that we have been exploring throughout the paper. We raise the possibility that certain decision theories, such as the ureilic likelihood theory, may be limited in their capacity to handle nonstandard likelihoods, where the ordering of options is not in accordance with their likelihoods. We explore this idea in the context of our example, where the likelihood is circular but can be reinterpreted as a linear likelihood with a 'tail' weighting. We ask whether it is possible to extend the concepts of standardness and likelihood to decision theories that go beyond the real number line, such as the decision theories based on Riemann surface or topological space. We conclude by noting that these decision theories are already capable of handling circular and nontransitive likelihoods. We speculate that a decision theory with a circular likelihood as a probability measure over a two-point space provides a model for human decision-making, where the ordering of options is not always in accordance with their likelihoods. We conclude by noting that our analysis has implications for artificial intelligence, where the decision-making capability of machines is influenced by their likelihood models. We speculate that a decision theory with a circular likelihood as a probability measure over a two-point space provides a model for both human and artificial decision-making. We conclude by noting that our analysis has implications for both natural and artificial decision-making, where the likelihood models play a crucial role.

The discovery of dark matter, a theoretical particle that constitutes most of the universe's mass, remains one of the unresolved mysteries in the field of particle physics. Typically, dark matter is thought to interact weakly with other particles, making it extremely difficult to detect. However, a new theory suggests that dark matter could be more massive and interact more strongly with other particles, potentially allowing for its detection in nuclear collisions. If this is the case, the dark matter interaction could be more easily identified if its breakdown occurs over a larger energy spectrum, rather than a single specific energy. Research suggests that dark matter interactions outside of a standard model of physics are more likely to be detected as collective electron and gamma-ray signals from astrophysical sources, rather than as a direct signal from space. In nuclear collisions, the direct detection of sub-GeV dark matter through an extended energy spectrum could be more than 10,000 times more probable than traditional direct detection methods, including those that utilize sensitive magnetic sensors and those that transform nuclear interactions into electric signals. Specifically, the direct detection of a new dark matter model with a 0.1 GeV mass and a 1 GeV mass has been found to have a 10,000 and a 700 times greater probability respectively, compared to a similar detection in a sensitive magnetic sensor experiment. Therefore, the examination of electron signals in nuclear collisions holds great promise as a method for identifying sub-GeV dark matter that interacts more strongly with other particles. This potential detection method, along with others such as astronomical observations and sensitive magnetic sensor experiments, should be utilized to search for dark matter in a wider energy range than currently thought necessary. Currently, scientists are exploring the electron signals resulting from the collision of lead atoms with high-energy protons at the Large Hadron Collider to identify the signals related to dark matter interactions, rather than focusing on detecting a single specific energy signal as in traditional direct detection experiments. Furthermore, this new approach is also being used to analyze data from experiments that have previously focused solely on sensitive magnetic sensor experiments, including one experiment that has collected 100 pb^-1 of data, without identifying the dark matter signal. As a result, this new theoretical framework has significantly expanded the possibilities for the identification of dark matter interactions. If the dark matter signal is detected in nuclear collisions, it would be the first confirmation of non-relativistic dark matter interaction through direct measurement and would also be the first evidence of dark matter being composed of massive particles that interact with other particles in a more pronounced way, rather than through indirect indicators

This paper investigates the dynamics of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where pair creation is disabled, for two initial states: a coherent state and a single-photon state. The study reveals that the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model exhibits Rabi oscillations to a greater extent than the Jaynes-Cummings model, particularly when using a two-mode squeezing state as the initial condition. Notably, this is in contrast to observations for a single-photon initial state, where the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model shows reduced Rabi oscillation compared to the Jaynes-Cummings model. Additionally, the study examines entanglement and transmission for both initial states, revealing that the entangulation of the system follows a different pattern for each state as time progresses, while transmission is largely dependent on the Hamming distance. Finally, this study compares the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model to the Jaynes-Cummings model and identifies key differences in their behaviors. The findings presented here are consistent with previously published research. The study utilizes Caldeira-Leggett model to derive the effective Hamiltonian for the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where the system's dissipation is minimized. The results obtained are accurate up to the optimal point. Notably, this point corresponds to the point of least interaction between the system and the environment in the Jaynes-Cummings model. The study hopes that these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model and the anti-Jaynes-Cummings quantum information processing system. The anti-Jaynes-Cummings model may offer an alternative solution for achieving a quantum memory with less influence from the environment, where the system's state remains nearly unchanged over an extended period. Furthermore, the study presents a method for quickly dephasing a qubit state, where the system's degree of entanglement with the continuum state varies depending on the qubit's state. The study hopes that this finding will contribute to the development of rapid quantum logic gates. The study also introduces a novel concept for quantum teleportation known as anti-teleportation, where anti-jumps are utilized to destroy the entanglement between the transfer qubit and the transfer register. The study demonstrates that anti-jumps can be achieved without being connected to the light field, which is in agreement with experimental findings using cold atoms. The study hopes that anti-teleportation will offer an innovative solution for achieving unconditional quantum teleportation, where the system's state is transferred without regard for its initial condition. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when the heart rate is high or variable. This paper proposes a new method for identifying IBIs that outperforms existing techniques. First, we transformed ECG signals into a higher dimension using a Tiramisu network, then applied a custom loss function to the transformed data. This was followed by identifying IBIs from the transformed data using a down-sampling approach. Once IBI locations are identified, the original signal is retrieved through back-propagation, and IBI intervals are recalculated. This method displays dynamic filter weights and variable activation patterns, effectively removing noise from the signals. As a result, this method achieves higher accuracy and signal clarity compared to existing techniques. Clinical data from both healthy individuals and patients with cardiovascular diseases were used to test the method's effectiveness, demonstrating significantly improved IBI identification and classification rates. This test confirmed that our method can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases with high accuracy. Overall, this method provides a superior alternative to existing techniques for measuring IBIs and has the potential to be a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying cardiovascular diseases. Code is available online at https://github.com/SajadMousavi/Tiramisu\_ECG. This work was based on research by Mousavi, S. et al. presented at IEEE RIVF 2020. Experimental data were obtained from PhysioNet: a resource for medical device and signal processing. Specifically, this research used datasets PFHH, Sudden Cardiac Death, and Cardiobit from PhysioNet. These datasets were used to test the method's effectiveness in identifying cardiovascular diseases through IBI identification. The method's performance in detecting cardiac diseases was evaluated using standard metrics such as sensitivity and specificity, demonstrating improved results compared to existing techniques. These results confirm that our method can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases with high accuracy. The corresponding author is Sajad Mousavi. This research introduces HUMBI, a comprehensive database of multiview human body gestures. Currently consisting of approximately 54,000 individual frames, 16,500 poses, and 2,300 distinct gesture categories, the collection is based on 144 unique gestures represented from multiple viewpoints. The HUMBI database can serve as a valuable asset for the development of advanced computer vision techniques, particularly those focused on multi-view learning and pose estimation. Additionally, the study includes details on a benchmarking competition involving state-of-the-art computer vision models, aimed at evaluating and comparing the performance of pose estimation algorithms on the HUMBI database. The competition encompasses two primary elements: a ranking-based challenge centered on the accuracy of predicted pose-quadruplets and a classification task involving the identification of distinct gesture categories. The winning approaches and corresponding results are presented. The HUMBI database, along with associated code and research outputs, can be accessed via the website given below. The task is to design the best estimator for $Y$ based on $X$ that minimizes its mean squared error (MSE). This is a classic problem of distributionally robust learning, solving a specialized version of \emph{conditional optimization problem}. We solve this by first deriving the \emph{Wasserstein-Gan} (WGAN) distance, and then applying it to construct a new loss function that allows us to tackle the original problem through conventional stochastic optimization. Our approach is evaluated using Monte-Carlo simulations, and we demonstrate that it yields superior performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art solutions. Even with significant advancements in NLP, many essential natural language processing tasks remain challenging or insoluble in certain languages due to limited training data. Researchers often employ costly data annotation or domain adaptation methods, moving source to target. Our study explores a more feasible approach, transferring knowledge from a high-resource language to a low-resource one, called cross-lingual transfer, without requiring synthetic data. We investigate if neural machine translation can facilitate this knowledge transfer by training a single task-oriented neural network on both the source and target languages. Our results show that this method performs well on three datasets across three languages, achieving success rates of 0.881, 0.912, and 0.935 in task-dependent evaluation; notably, it surpasses or matches state-of-the-art performance in cross-lingual transfer while being easier to execute and requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our method promotes multi-lingual compatibility and demonstrate its applicability to new, unseen tasks through a series of experiments including task adaptations. Ultimately, we show that our cross-lingual transfer method offers weak guidance that can improve the performance of self-supervised, model-independent baselines, solidifying its value in low-resource and limited-data scenarios. Related code is available at https://github.com/aleju/nld.eyJ.

A common approach to video super-resolution is the in-video alignment technique, where the network shifts each frame relative to a reference frame to create corresponding labels. However, this method is prone to errors when the network tries to move frames beyond their physical boundaries. To address this issue, we have developed a novel learning scheme that directly learns the motion between videos in a self-consistent manner, unaffected by external alignment techniques. We've also introduced an alternative label generation method that produces more accurate results by only moving selected pixels instead of entire frames. Our new algorithm, BasicVSR++, uses a simplified architecture with fewer channels and fewer layers, achieving better performance than previous approaches without sacrificing detail. When combined with our novel training method, BasicVSR++ outperforms other state-of-the-art models in video super-resolution tasks. We've also conducted thorough analyses on our dataset, LSR, which is optimized for VR applications and contains high-quality 8K videos alongside their lower resolution counterparts. Our model is now available on OpenSource. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. When evaluated on the LSR dataset, BasicVSR++ achieved an PSNR of 38.32, an SSIM of 0.944, and an MS-SSIM of 0.883, representing a significant improvement of 3.53, 3.14, and 2.64 respectively over the current best model. To put it simply, BasicVSR++ performed 3.53% better in terms of PSNR, 3.14% better in terms of SSIM, and 2.64% better in terms of MS-SSIM. To evaluate the model's generalizability, we also tested it on other popular VR datasets and achieved comparable results. Our model is now available on OpenSource. In complex environments, like medical intervention, most reinforcement learning tasks are long-term challenges. Currently, deep reinforcement learning solutions are limited to single tasks or simple multi-task learning with separate skill modules. Yet, to effectively learn complex, interconnected tasks like robotic surgery, we need to train a single agent to handle multiple tasks efficiently. This paper introduces a novel approach to deep multi-task reinforcement learning using modular systems that train sub-tasks separately but interconnectedly. To improve handling of novel situations, we've also developed a novel method for sub-task connection based on shared features. In a simulated surgical training environment, our proposed system showed a significant improvement in learning speed and a more stable training process over non-modular and linearly-structured multi-task training methods. Additionally, our system demonstrated more efficient use of computational resources than single-task training methods. Overall, our results indicate that our modular system achieves faster learning and better adaptation to novel situations compared to traditional multi-task training methods. You can find the code and environment setup to replicate the results in this link: https://github.com/Chen-UIUC/Modular-MDTL. Additionally, a video showcasing the trained agent's performance in a simulated surgical setting is available here: https://youtu.be/8a_2yH1V0Hk. By applying Clifford analysis principles, we subsequently prove an analogous result for Dirac operators. In doing so, we provide a novel expression for the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operators on R^n+1 step-by-step. Furthermore, we establish a circumferential formula for these eigenfunctions, followed by a comprehensive discussion of the monotonicity of their first positive eigenvalue in accordance with a circumferential metric. In addition, we explicitly calculate the circumferential first positive eigenvalue of the Dirac operators, thereby resolving a longstanding problem initially posed by Dryden and Gong. Our findings also enable us to derive an inequality for the first positive eigenvalue of the Dirac operators in accordance with a circumferential metric. Recent studies have focused on entropy measures in one-dimensional conservative systems with a planar symmetry, developing the Dyck framework for defining chaos sets based on path deviations from a central line. Using this approach, two entropy-like measures can be calculated: $h_{\mathrm{D}}$, which quantifies area associated with diverging trajectories, and $h_{\mathrm{P}}$, which measures path-related entropy. Applied to the heterochaos baker map, a piecewise linear system with a straight boundary, the Dyck framework provides a method for defining chaos sets and calculating their associated entropies. Furthermore, studies have found that when the system's parameter satisfies a specific inequality, the entropy associated with approaching a straight boundary is not achieved, while numerical investigations indicate that this phenomenon is a general effect in one-dimensional conservative systems with planar symmetry. Importantly, as the system's parameter reaches a critical value, its entropy-related approach to a straight boundary ceases to increase over time, instead transitioning to a complex, sanaky-shaped pattern. This behavior has been observed in other systems with a planar symmetry, such as the Chirikov standard map, and is found to be robust under variations in system's parameter and initial conditions. Additionally, studies have established a connection between the proposed Dyck framework and existing research on chaos sets in system's phase space. Lastly, as a validation of the proposed method, studies have compared the entropy values calculated using the Dyck approach with those obtained from traditional chaos measures, demonstrating that the proposed method generates results aligned with existing research. These findings open the door for future applications of the Dyck approach in studying chaos phenomena in one-dimensional conservative systems with planar symmetry. Conversely, studies have revealed that this framework is insufficient for modeling two-dimensional systems with a planar symmetry, as it fails to capture certain types of chaotic behavior observed in these systems. Instead, studies have proposed an alternative method for defining chaos sets, one that incorporates not only path-related data, but also spatial considerations. This approach, built upon a combination of the Dyck framework and other existing concepts, enables a more comprehensive understanding of chaos phenomena in two-dimensional systems with a planar symmetry. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that the proposed method generates results aligned with other, related research. These findings have established a new paradigm for studying chaos phenomena in one-dimensional conservative systems with planar symmetry. Furthermore, studies have revealed that this paradigm can be extended to and validated in various applications, as well as across distinct variants of the heterochaos baker map

This paper presents a generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an autoregressive method using pitch-sensitive Dilate Convolution Neural Network to model raw audio signals. The framework generates quasi-periodic patterns at a chosen pitch, then combines them with a transient component to produce high-quality raw audio signals in real-time. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through two applications: transferring the pitch of a melodic piano audio clip and generating synthetic brokendisk sounds, showcasing its capabilities in modeling complex raw audio signals. Evaluation metrics such as Mean Absolute Error and Multi-Scale Signal to Distortion Ratio are used to analyze the generated signals. The results of continuous pitch transfer reveal a low MAE of 0.0077, MCSDR of 2.34, and a wide applicable pitch range, while the synthesized brokendisk sounds exhibit a high degree of realism with consistent spectral patterns across different periods. The framework is open-source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/yindengyong/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. The demo video of Quasi-Periodic WaveNet can be found at https://youtu.be/FW9T0sHxI7Y. The generated audio files are uploaded to Audio1Source at https://audio1source.org?audio=quasi_periodic_wavenet. The framework's performance in modeling raw audio signals contributes to the development of end-to-end, pitch-constrained neural vocoders. The research has potential implications for future work in neural audio synthesis, particularly in the area of end-to-end, pitch-controlled neural vocoders. The authors explore the limitations of the framework in modeling non-quasi-periodic patterns and suggest future research directions to tackle this challenge. Future studies could utilize the QP-WN framework as a pre-trained model, incorporating additional training data and techniques such as self-supervised learning and contrastive learning to improve its performance in modeling raw audio signals. Additionally, future work could involve modifying the framework to model non-quasi-periodic patterns by integrating multiple QP-WN components with diverse pitch values, as well as exploring the utilization of QP-WN in combination with pre-generated periodical components. The authors emphasize the need for future research in tackling the technical challenges of modeling raw audio signals and encourage the community to contribute to the development of a reliable end-to-end, pitch-constrained neural vocoder. Large-scale recommender systems rely on a sophisticated method called collaborative filtering (CF) to address user preference uncertainty, information scarcity, and groupability. This research introduces a innovative CF algorithm termed BUCF that addresses these challenges by leveraging the concepts of spatial autocorrelation, spatial filtering, and data segmentation. BUCF generates biclusters composed of users and items with high preference coherence, and then applies spatial analysis to model each group's preference patterns. BUCF treats each bicuster as a unitary variable with a multivariate normal distribution, training on a latent space while downscaling external noise. Theoretical justifications and extensive experiments demonstrate that BUCF surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in preserving global preference patterns, accurately predicting long-tail items, and accommodating subjective user preferences. Moreover, the development of BUCf includes the provision of an open-source implementation framework. This study delves into the fundamental relationship between spatial filtering and bicustering, and presents a novel theoretical framework that highlights the advantages of integrating these concepts. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of dataset characteristics and algorithm performance is offered to shed light on the paradoxes and limitations of CF in modeling user preferences. The presence of magnetic activity in solar spectra affects observations, but its impact can be difficult to predict.  This study aimed to determine the impact of magnetic activity on solar spectra using data from the HARPS-N solar instrument.  To achieve this, researchers analyzed in-depth HARPS-N data for three solar-like stars with magnetic activity characteristics similar to the Sun.  This was accomplished by utilizing advanced techniques, including machine learning algorithms and spectral imaging.  As a result, researchers identified four new activity indicators for solar spectra and confirmed the significance of existing indicators.  Through these findings, researchers gained a deeper understanding of the roots of activity patterns in solar spectra and the impact of magnetic activity on observations.  This research has applications in searching for biosignatures in exoplanet transmission spectra by identifying potential signs of artificial signals and reducing their impact. To observe a Majorana zero mode, we suggest a tunneling spectroscopy method that involves coupling the affected leg of an Ab-stacked InAs/Sb/InAs quantum dot to a resistive material like Pd or Au through an ohmic connection. The technique relies on the distinct dissipative properties of MZMs versus other possible zero modes. Specifically, we propose that MZMs, being topological in nature, have highly conductive characteristics associated with Luttinger liquids, whereas other modes will exhibit varying degrees of dissipative behaviors. By utilizing a resistive electrode in tunneling spectroscopy, we aim to investigate the dissipative nature of zero modes and, by extension, gain a better understanding of the quantum and phases of these modes. Our method also includes various tunneling setups as options, with the primary goal of differentiating between MZMs and other modes and ultimately validating the observed phenomena through experimental analysis. Possible interpretations of failure and future experimental directions are also a focus of this proposed approach. Furthermore, we suggest that MZMs, having highly conductive characteristics, would exhibit signifying spectral features such as bifurcation, symmetry, and phase-coherence at zero bias, as opposed to other modes, which may either lack these features or display varying degrees of these characteristics. By tuning the tunneling bias to positive values, we anticipate that MZMs will demonstrate reduced tunneling currents relative to other modes, with the latter exhibiting varying tunneling behaviors. Our proposed tunneling spectra, consisting of tunneling conductivity as a function of bias, would distinguish between MZMs and other modes by identifying signatures of phase-coherence and Kondo peaks within these spectra. By tuning the electrode height above the quantum dot, we expect to observe an ohmic dissolution of contact with the affected leg, resulting in a tunneling current characteristic of Luttinger liquids, with the associated spectra featuring bifurcation, phase-coherence, and Kondo peaks. By incorporating numerical simulations using a Luttinger liquid model, we demonstrate that these predicted features would indeed emerge, with the associated spectra showing reduced tunneling currents relative to other modes. Our proposed approach, therefore, offers a potential solution to differentiating MZMs from other modes and observing the associated zero-bias peaks. This approach is also tested on specific examples of groups and comonads.

category theory itself. This method may have additional uses and applications

Recent advancements in image processing research, spurred by advancements in deep learning, have yielded impressive results, particularly in image restoration tasks. This paper investigates the development of a single, versatile neural network to perform both forward and reverse tone mapping on general images. Unlike existing solutions that analyze a single image, our model is designed to extract a style from a collection of multiple images, ultimately enabling it to produce a harmonious, naturally-colored output from monochromatic data in a more effective manner. Additionally, our model can reverse the colorization process applied to images by analyzing a colored image and identifying a suitable monochromatic style. This unique ability sets our model apart from existing techniques and expands its potential applications. Extensive testing of our model on the CMOS image sensor dataset has shown promising results, with subjective evaluations confirming its ability to produce more natural colors on a wider range of subjects. The code for our model is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. This paper has been accepted for publication at the CVPR 2021 conference. The associated demo video can be found on the YouTube platform.

This report outlines the rules and evaluation criteria for the CVPR 2022 Low-Vision Electrocution Underwater Augmented Quadcopter Racing Through Corners (LOVEU AQTC R) challenge. The loveu project aims to make existing quadcopter racing games accessible to visually impaired individuals by incorporating audio cues and providing them with the skills to navigate these circuits. The key obstacle in this context is the presence of blind spots or 'corners' throughout the racing track. To address this, we have introduced a new challenge within the loveu project, focusing on detecting these corners and accurately positioning the quadcopter to avoid collisions. The AQTC R challenge represents a critical advancement in this mission as it requires the development of more sophisticated strategies to effectively navigate the quadcopter through the corners of these tracks. The evaluation process will be based on the timing of the quadcopter as it completes a lap, with faster times indicating better performance. The report provides a detailed outline of the track used in the competition, the parameters for the simulation environment, the data format of the track files, and the evaluation criteria of the loveu AQTC R challenge. The competition website hosting the dataset, as well as the quadcopter racing simulation environment, can be found at https://loveu.github.io/cvpr2022-qrac/. Events detected at High Momentum Detector (HMD) within Beam-Particle Test (BPT) facility consist of sparse point-like information which can be greatly enhanced through reconstruction. Our improvement on 3D Sparse Time Projection Chamber (3D-SPTC) reconstruction technique has shown significant reduction in reconstructed event volume, thereby decreasing computation costs by a factor of up to 400. This optimized approach utilizes a Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) that compresses raw track data while retaining essential features to facilitate efficient inversion of a parameterised model, thereby enabling precise track quality assessment and recovery of original tracks. Our analysis based on BPT data demonstrates the superiority of 3D-SPTC over 2D-based methods in terms of both reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, our novel strategy facilitates real-time real-world applications of HMD, showcasing its potential for widespread use in future particle accelerator systems. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub for public review. According to flux-conservative methods in computational fluid dynamics, shock collapse in a density gradient medium has been shown to lead to nonphysical results, particularly when using Godunov-type methods. This paper reexamines the issue and provides alternative solutions. It first identifies the source of the problem, which arises from incomplete reconstruction of cells behind the shock, and proposes a method to improve spatial accuracy for conservative Riemann solvers. An alternative approach is also offered, utilizing a zeroth-order conservative method that does not rely on flux approximation and instead directly calculates conserved quantities. Numerical examples are used to demonstrate the performance of the new methods. Furthermore, this paper confirms the findings of previous studies and provides a clearer understanding of the required conditions for nonphysical results to occur. Finally, an exploration is undertaken of how to generalize these new methods to higher-dimensional scenarios. Overall, this paper contributes to the development of reliable and accurate methods for simulating shock collapse in density gradient environments. Numerical simulations of various problems, including a baricenter test, a selfsimilar problem and an 2D and 3D Sedov problem are presented to demonstrate the efficiency of the new methods. Finally, this paper delves into the generalization and implementation of these new methods in higher-dimensional contexts. In particular, it focuses on the development of a three-dimensional conservative method using the quasi-conservative approach. To evaluate its performance, a range of test cases, including baricenter and Sedov problems in two and three dimensions, were utilized. An in-depth examination of the success of the new methods is also included. Additionally, this paper investigates the underlying cause of shock collapse in density gradient mediums and how it might be extended to more complex scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we draw a comparison with requirement engineering, an established field, to propose using user-centric approaches in explanation specification. The systematic evaluation of our approach, using a practical example based on online shopping, has yielded promising results, thereby solidifying the foundation of a user-focused methodology for explanation specification. This approach, grounded in requirement engineering, emerges as a viable option for addressing the current and future challenges related to explainable AI. Current correlations in microscopic models can be captured through a probability space where a current vector and a parameter space are defined. A linear mapping is applied to both the current vector and the parameter space, resulting in scaled versions of both, which allows for the examination of model variations and scaling effects. This transformation is performed to explore the scalability of current distributions and the scalability of their associated fluctuations in random thermodynamic systems. By applying transformation principles, we demonstrate the scalability of second-moment characteristics such as the spectral density and correlation functions, which remains invariant under the scaling of both the current vector and the parameter space. This result is illustrated through two specific examples: a random bond ER model and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process combined with a Markov chain. The application of this transformation in Section 2 allows for a comprehensive analysis of the spectral density and correlation functions in models that cannot be exactly solved in their standard form, as shown in Section 3 with the ER model and Stochastic Block Model. The latter's results reveal a notable correlation existing between a normalized spectral density and a squared correlation value that reaches a maximum of 1, or 100%, in the block-size limit. The ER model's results, on the other hand, reveal a decay rate of 1/(2L), where L is the system's size, which itself becomes unbounded as L grows. The same rate of decay is observed in the OR model; however, when the current vector is scaled differently, the decay rate becomes 1/L and the normalized spectral density reaches a minimum of 2/sqrt(L) in the size limit. The combination of these two systems, the OR model and the Markov chain, yields a spectral density with linearly decreasing values at zero frequency and the correlation at non-zero frequency reaching a minimum of 1/2L when normalized by the square of the spectral density itself. The same analysis is applied to the MCM model in Section 4, which reveals a decay rate of 1/L and a minimum correlation of 1/2L when the spectral density is not at zero frequency. The last two models analyzed in this study were the interaction of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a Markov chain and an autoregressive process of order 4. The latter revealed a non-monotonic but decaying correlation over time and the other combination also displayed a non-monotonic but decaying correlation over time. The time-dependent nature of these correlations was examined in detail, which in turn led to a discussion on scaling effects

We establish a coherence theorem for the Milnor fibration in a specific context, 
which can be viewed as a straightforward extension of Gómez-Mont's coherence theorem 
for Milnor algebras in dimensions two and three, or equivalently, a direct extension 
of the flatness coherence theorem proven by S. L. Regazzoni. In order to achieve this 
extension, we identify a coherent condition related to the flatness of the critical 
locus, applicable to any hypersurface singularity defined by a polynomial in four 
variables. Furthermore, we derive a simple, explicit condition for flatness that 
applies not just to critical loci but also to any projective closure of these loci, 
thus generalizing a previous result of B. Fryer's thesis and providing a novel, 
non-algebraic approach to this problem. Finally, we apply our findings to not only 
Milnor fibers but also other related spaces, such as the Minimally Extended 
Fiberings and the links of these spaces, thereby covering cases beyond those 
covered by Gómez-Mont's coherence theorem. In the process, we also derive a 
novel, non-algebraic condition for flatness of a projective curve, which may be

proponentially broken, thereby allowing for a practical, computationally
